In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Sad is Meccan according to all scholars, and it has eighty-six verses. It is also said to have eighty-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ (1) ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ (2) ﴿How many a generation We destroyed before them, and they cried out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ (3)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Sad﴾. The common reading is "Ṣ" with the dal pronounced with a jazm (sukun) because of pausing, since it is one of the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijā'), like "Alif Lam Mim" and "Alif Lam Mim Ra." Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn 'Asim read "Ṣādi" with a kasra on the dal and without tanwin.

For this reading there are two views (madhhabān).

The first is that it derives from ṣādā, yuṣādī, meaning "to oppose" (ʿāraḍa). From it comes Allah's words: ﴿As for him who is rich, you attend to him eagerly﴾ [ʿAbasa: 6], meaning "you present yourself to him." Al-muṣādāh is opposition, and from it comes al-ṣadā, which is the echo that answers the voice in empty places. So the meaning is: "Oppose the Qur'an with your deeds, answer it with them, act upon its commands, and refrain from what it forbids." Al-Nahhas said: This view is reported from al-Hasan, who explained his reading with it as a sound transmission (riwāyah ṣaḥīḥah). It is also reported from him that the meaning is: "Recite it and present yourself to its recitation."

The second view is that the dal is kasra because of the meeting of two sakin letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn).

Isa ibn 'Umar read "Ṣāda" with a fatḥa on the dal, like "Qāf" and "Nūn" with a fatḥa on their final letters. For this reading there are three views. The first is that it means "recite" (utlu). The second is that it was given a fatḥa because of the meeting of two sakin letters, and he preferred the fatḥa for assimilation (ittibā') and because it is the lightest of the vowels. The third is that it is in the accusative by way of an oath without a particle, like your saying: "Allah, I will certainly do it." It is also said that it is in the accusative by way of incitement (al-ighrā'). It is also said that the meaning is: Muhammad ﷺ won over the hearts of the creation and attracted them until they believed in him.

Ibn Abi Ishaq also read "Ṣādin" with a kasra on the dal and tanwin, on the basis that it is in the genitive by omission of the particle of oath. This is far-fetched, although Sibawayh permitted something similar. It may also be that it is treated like those words that do not take full inflection, such as sounds and other things.

Harun al-A'war and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read "Ṣādu," "Qāfu," and "Nūnu" with a ḍamma on their final letters, because it is the form known for indeclinability (binā') in most cases, as in mundhu, qaṭṭu, qablu and baʿdu. And when you make "Ṣ" the name of the surah, it is not declined (lam yanṣarif), just as when you name a feminine thing with a masculine name it is not declined, even if its letters are few.

Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah were asked about "Ṣ," and both said: "We do not know what it is."

Ikrima said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about "Ṣ," and he said: "Ṣ" was a sea in Mecca, and the Throne of the Merciful was upon it, when there was neither night nor day.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Ṣ" is a sea by which Allah will bring the dead to life between the two blasts.

Al-Dahhak said: Its meaning is "Allah has spoken truly" (ṣadaqa Allāh).

It is also reported from him that "Ṣ" is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names, may He be exalted.

Al-Suddi said, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas as well.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is the key to the names of Allah, the Eternal Refuge (Ṣamad), the Maker of created things (Ṣāni' al-maṣnū'āt), and the One true to His promise (Ṣādiq al-wa'd).

Qatada said: It is one of the names of the Merciful. It is also reported from him that it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

Mujahid said: It is the opening of the surah.

It is also said: It is among the things which Allah has kept to Himself in knowledge, and this is the meaning of the first view.

All of this has been mentioned before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 155, second or third edition.]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the Qur'an﴾. It is in the genitive by the oath particle wāw, and the wāw replaces the bāʾ. He swears by the Qur'an to draw attention to its great rank, for in it is the explanation of everything, a cure for what is in the breasts, and a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿Full of reminder﴾ is in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt), and the sign of its genitive is the yāʾ, since it is a defective noun (ism muʿtall), and its original form is dhawā on the pattern faʿala. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: The meaning of "full of reminder" is full of clarification (dhī al-bayān). Al-Dahhak said: full of honour, meaning whoever believes in it will have honour in both abodes, as Allah says: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10], meaning your honour. Also, the Qur'an is noble in itself because of its inimitability and because it contains what nothing else contains. It is also said: "Full of reminder" means that it contains mention of what is needed of the matters of religion. It is also said: it contains mention of the names of Allah and His glorification. It is also said: meaning full of admonition and remembrance.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and there are several views about it.

It is said that the answer to the oath is "Ṣ," because its meaning is "true" (ḥaqq), so it is the answer to the phrase "And the Qur'an," just as you say: "Truly, by Allah," "He descended, by Allah," "It is obligatory, by Allah." In this case, pausing on "And the Qur'an, full of reminder" is good (ḥasan), and pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is complete (tamām). Ibn al-Anbari said this, and al-Tha'labi transmitted its meaning from al-Farra'.

It is also said: the answer is "Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition," because "bal" (nay, but) negates something that came before and affirms something else. This was said by al-Qutabi, so it is as if he said: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition against accepting the truth and in enmity toward Muhammad ﷺ." Or it is: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — the matter is not as they say, that you are a sorcerer and a liar, for they know you for truthfulness and trustworthiness; rather they are proud and refuse to accept the truth." This is like His words: ﴿Qāf. By the glorious Qur'an. Nay, but they wonder﴾ [Qāf: 1–2].

It is also said: the answer is ﴿How many a generation We destroyed﴾ [Qāf: 36], as if he said: "By the Qur'an, how many We destroyed," and when the particle "kam" came after, the lām was removed from it, like His words: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9], meaning "indeed he has succeeded." Al-Mahdawi said: This is the view of al-Farra'. Ibn al-Anbari said: On this view, pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is not complete.

Al-Akhfash said: The answer to the oath is "Indeed all of them denied the Messengers, so My punishment was justified," and similar to it is His words: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 97], and His words: "By the heaven and the night-visitant," up to His words ﴿Indeed every soul...﴾ [al-Tariq: 1–4]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them, and the verses and stories are many.

Al-Kisa'i said: The answer to the oath is His words: ﴿Indeed that is true, the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is uglier than the first, because the speech is even longer between the oath and its answer.

It is also said that the answer is His words: ﴿Indeed this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54].

Qatada said: The answer is omitted, and its estimate is: "By the Qur'an full of reminder, you will certainly be resurrected," and similar to it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, meaning in pride and refusal to accept the truth, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," the arrogance takes him to sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206]. In the language of the Arabs, "ʿizzah" means domination and subjugation. It is said: "Whoever is mighty plunders," meaning whoever overcomes despoils. From it comes: ﴿And he has overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23], meaning he overcame me. Jarir said:

*He prevails over the road with his shoulders,*
*as the dispossessed gambler prevails over the arrows.* [The line describes a camel that prevails over the other camels in keeping to the road, and urges onward, and compares his eagerness to keep the road and to press on with the eagerness of this dispossessed gambler to cast the arrows, hoping to recover some of what he lost of his wealth. The *khalī'* is the one stripped of his property and crushed.]

He meant: prevails. "And opposition" means in showing disagreement and opposition. It comes from *shiqq* (a side), as if this is on one side and that on the other. This was explained fully before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 2, p. 143, second edition.]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many a generation We destroyed before them﴾, meaning peoples who were more powerful than these. "Kam" is a word of multiplicity. ﴿And they cried out﴾, meaning with pleas for help and repentance. Calling out (al-nidā') is raising the voice, and from it comes the report: "Throw it to Bilal, for he is louder in voice than you," meaning higher.

﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Hasan said: They called out in repentance, but it was not the time for repentance, nor a time when deeds would benefit. Al-Nahhas said: This is his explanation of the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "but it was no time for escape." As for Israel, he narrated from Abu Ishaq, from al-Taymi, from Ibn 'Abbas: "But it was no time for escape." He said: It was not a time for leaping (nazw), which is a kind of running, nor for fleeing. He said: They were all restrained. Al-Kalbi said: When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others: "Manāṣ," meaning: "You must flee and be defeated." But when the punishment came upon them, they said: "Manāṣ." Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Qushayri said: On this view, the estimate is: "They called out, 'Manāṣ,'" and it was omitted because the rest of the speech indicates it, meaning: it is not the time for what you call out for. There is some arbitrariness in this, since it is far-fetched to say that every generation that perished used to say "Manāṣ" when compelled.

It is also said: The meaning of "But it was no time for escape" is: "But it was no time for deliverance," and it is in the accusative by the negation of *lā* (lā li-khalāṣ) acting on it. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this, because on this view there is no meaning for the wāw in "But it was no time for escape." Al-Jurjani said: That is, "they called out when there was no escape," meaning an hour in which there is no refuge and no escape. Since he placed "lā" first and delayed "ḥīn," that required the wāw, just as the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) requires it when it is made an inceptive sentence and a predicate. Like your saying: "Zayd came riding," but when you make it an inceptive sentence and predicate, it requires the wāw, as in "Zayd came to me while he was riding." So "ḥīn" is an adverb of time for His words: "they called out."

"Manāṣ" means retreat, flight, and deliverance. That is, they called out seeking deliverance at a time when there was no deliverance for them. Al-Farra' said:

*Is it from the mention of Layla, when she removed herself from you, and you became hesitant?* [The full line: *"...fa-taqṣuru ʿanhā khaṭwatan wa-tabūṣu,"* meaning: "so you fall short of her by a step and go forward."]

It is said: *nāṣa ʿan qirnihi yanūṣu nawṣan wa-manāṣan*, meaning he fled and turned aside. Al-Nahhas said: It is also said: *nāṣa yanūṣu* when he advanced. I say: On this view, it is among the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād). *Al-nawṣ* is the wild donkey. *Istanāṣa* means he drew back, as al-Jawhari said.

The grammarians have discussed "But it was no time" and the pause upon it, and Abu 'Ubayda al-Qasim ibn Sallam expanded on this in his book on the readings, but nearly all he said is rejected, except for a few points. Sibawayh said: "Lāt" is made similar to "laysa," and its subject is a pronoun, meaning: "Our times are not a time of escape." He related that some of the Arabs put it in the nominative, saying: "wa-lātu ḥīnin manāṣ" [and it is no time for escape]. He related that the nominative is rare, and the predicate is omitted just as the subject was omitted in the accusative, meaning: "and it is no time for escape for us." The pause upon it, according to Sibawayh and al-Farra', is on "lāt" with a tāʾ, then one begins with "ḥīna manāṣ." This is the view of Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan said: The view is as Sibawayh said, because it is made similar to "laysa," so just as one says "laysat," one says "lāt."

The pause upon it according to al-Kisa'i is with a hā': "lāh." This is the view of al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid. Ali ibn Sulayman related from him that the proof for this is that a hā' was added to it for the feminization of the word, just as one says "thumma" (then) becoming "thummah," and "rubba" (perhaps) becoming "rubbah." Al-Qushayri said: It is also said "thumat" meaning "thumma," and "rubbat" meaning "rubba," so they added a hā' to "lā," saying "lāh," just as they said with "thummah," at the pause it becomes a tāʾ.

Al-Tha'labi said: The people of the language said: "Lāt ḥīn" are two words with fatḥa, as if they were one word, and it is only "lā" with a tāʾ added to it, like "rubba" and "rubbat," and "thumma" and "thummat." Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i said:

*They sought our reconciliation, but it was not the time,*
*and we answered that it is not a time for survival.*

Another said:

*Remembrance of the love of Layla has come to you, no longer in time,*
*and old age has come and cut off the companion.*

Among the Arabs there are those who put "lāt" in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*So you will surely recognize people subdued,*
*and you will surely regret, and it is no time for regret.*

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash held that the *ta'* in *wa-lāta ḥīn* is separate from *ḥīn*, and they said its meaning is *wa-laysat* ("and it was not"). The same is written in the new and old *maṣāḥif* (copies of the Qur'an), with the *ta'* separated from *ḥīn*. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna also held this view.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: "In my view, the pause (*waqf*) on this word is on *wa-lā*, and the new start is *taḥīna manāṣ*, so the *ta'* is joined to *ḥīn*." Some said: "*Lāt*," then he starts again with "*ḥīna manāṣ*."

Al-Mahdawi said: Abu 'Ubayd mentioned that the *ta'* in the *muṣḥaf* is joined to *ḥīn*, and this is an error according to the grammarians (*naḥwiyyīn*), and it contradicts the view of the exegetes (*mufassirīn*). Abu 'Ubayd's argument was that he said: "We have not found the Arabs adding this *ta'* except to *ḥīn*, *awān* and *al-ān*." He cited Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

*"Al-'ātifūna taḥīna mā min 'āṭifin… wa-l-muṭ'imūna zamāna Ibn al-Muṭ'am"*

He cited Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i:

*"Ṭalabū ṣulḥanā wa-lāta awāni… fa-ajabnā an laysa ḥīna baqā'"*

So he added the *ta'* to *awān*. Abu 'Ubayd said: From their adding the *ta'* to *al-ān* is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both). A man asked him about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), and he mentioned his virtues, then said: "Take it with you *talān*." Likewise is the saying of the poet [[It is Jamil ibn Ma'mar, and after it:
"Indeed the best of those who connect in purity… is the one who meets his beloved wherever they are."]]:

*"Nuwallī qabla nay'i dārī Jumānā… wa-ṣilīnā kamā zaʿamti talānā"*

Abu 'Ubayd said: Despite all of this, I deliberately looked at what is called the *imam* (the *muṣḥaf* of 'Uthman), and I found the *ta'* joined with *ḥīn*, written as *taḥīn*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: As for the first verse which Abu Wajza cited, the scholars of language transmitted it in four ways, all of them contrary to what he cited. In one of them there are two interpretations. Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) transmitted it as:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta mā min 'āṭif"*

The second transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta ḥīna ta'āṭufin"*

The third transmission was narrated by Ibn Kaysan:

*"Al-'āṭifūnah ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

He made it a *hā'* in pause and a *tā'* in continuous speech (*idrāj*), and he claimed that it is to show the vowel (*li-bayān al-ḥaraka*), being likened to the feminine *hā'*. The fourth transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūnahu ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

In this transmission there are two interpretations. One of them, which is the view of Isma'il ibn Ishaq, is that the *hā'* is in the accusative position, as you say: *al-ḍāribūna Zaydan*; when you use a pronoun you say: *al-ḍāribūhu*. Sibawayh permitted in poetry *al-ḍāribūnahu*, so Isma'il gave the feminine form following Sibawayh's permission of its like. The other interpretation is that the *hā'* is to show the vowel, as you say: *marra bina al-muslimūnah* in pause, and then in continuous speech it is treated as it is in pause, as the people of Madina recited: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ ۝ هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28–29] ("My wealth has not benefited me; my authority has perished from me").

As for the second verse, there is no proof in it, because it is paused upon as: *(wa-lāta awān)*. However, there is a difficulty in it, because it is transmitted as *(wa-lāta awānin)* with the genitive (*khafḍ*), whereas what follows *lāta* is only nominative or accusative. Although it has been transmitted from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he recited *"wa-lāti ḥīnin manāṣ"* with a kasra on the *tā'* of *lāt* and on the *nūn* of *ḥīn*, the established reading from him is that he recited *"wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ"*, so he built *lāt* on the kasra and put *ḥīn* in the accusative. As for *(wa-lāta awān)*, it has two interpretations. Al-Akhfash said: there is a hidden element in it, meaning *wa-lāta ḥīna awān*.

Al-Nahhas said: This view is clearly wrong. The other interpretation, from Abu Ishaq, said: its meaning is *wa-lāta awānunā*, so he deleted the *muḍāf ilayh* (the noun annexed to), and therefore it was required that it not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), and he gave it a kasra because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited it as *(wa-lāta awānu)* with a *ḍamma*.

As for the third verse, it is a later (*muwallad*) verse whose composer is unknown, and no proof can be established by it. Moreover, Muhammad ibn Yazid transmitted it as *(kamā zaʿamti al-āna)*. Others said: the meaning is *kamā zaʿamti anti al-āna*, so he dropped the *hamza* from *anti* and the *nūn*. As for his argument from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, when he mentioned the virtues of 'Uthman to the man and said to him: "Take it with you *talān* to your companions," there is no proof in it, because the transmitter only narrates this according to its meaning. The evidence for this is that Mujahid narrates this hadith from Ibn 'Umar and says in it: "Go and strive your utmost." Another narrated it: "Take it with you *al-āna*." As for his argument that he found it in the *Imam* as *"taḥīnu"*, there is no proof in it, because the meaning of *Imam* is that it is the leader of the *maṣāḥif*; if it opposes them, then it is not their *imam*, and in all the *maṣāḥif* it is *"wa-lāta"*. So if there were nothing in this but this argument, it would be convincing.

The plural of *manāṣ* is *manāwiṣ*.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the Qur'an﴾. It is in the genitive by the oath particle wāw, and the wāw replaces the bāʾ. He swears by the Qur'an to draw attention to its great rank, for in it is the explanation of everything, a cure for what is in the breasts, and a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿Full of reminder﴾ is in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt), and the sign of its genitive is the yāʾ, since it is a defective noun (ism muʿtall), and its original form is dhawā on the pattern faʿala. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: The meaning of "full of reminder" is full of clarification (dhī al-bayān). Al-Dahhak said: full of honour, meaning whoever believes in it will have honour in both abodes, as Allah says: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10], meaning your honour. Also, the Qur'an is noble in itself because of its inimitability and because it contains what nothing else contains. It is also said: "Full of reminder" means that it contains mention of what is needed of the matters of religion. It is also said: it contains mention of the names of Allah and His glorification. It is also said: meaning full of admonition and remembrance.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and there are several views about it.

It is said that the answer to the oath is "Ṣ," because its meaning is "true" (ḥaqq), so it is the answer to the phrase "And the Qur'an," just as you say: "Truly, by Allah," "He descended, by Allah," "It is obligatory, by Allah." In this case, pausing on "And the Qur'an, full of reminder" is good (ḥasan), and pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is complete (tamām). Ibn al-Anbari said this, and al-Tha'labi transmitted its meaning from al-Farra'.

It is also said: the answer is "Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition," because "bal" (nay, but) negates something that came before and affirms something else. This was said by al-Qutabi, so it is as if he said: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition against accepting the truth and in enmity toward Muhammad ﷺ." Or it is: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — the matter is not as they say, that you are a sorcerer and a liar, for they know you for truthfulness and trustworthiness; rather they are proud and refuse to accept the truth." This is like His words: ﴿Qāf. By the glorious Qur'an. Nay, but they wonder﴾ [Qāf: 1–2].

It is also said: the answer is ﴿How many a generation We destroyed﴾ [Qāf: 36], as if he said: "By the Qur'an, how many We destroyed," and when the particle "kam" came after, the lām was removed from it, like His words: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9], meaning "indeed he has succeeded." Al-Mahdawi said: This is the view of al-Farra'. Ibn al-Anbari said: On this view, pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is not complete.

Al-Akhfash said: The answer to the oath is "Indeed all of them denied the Messengers, so My punishment was justified," and similar to it is His words: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 97], and His words: "By the heaven and the night-visitant," up to His words ﴿Indeed every soul...﴾ [al-Tariq: 1–4]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them, and the verses and stories are many.

Al-Kisa'i said: The answer to the oath is His words: ﴿Indeed that is true, the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is uglier than the first, because the speech is even longer between the oath and its answer.

It is also said that the answer is His words: ﴿Indeed this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54].

Qatada said: The answer is omitted, and its estimate is: "By the Qur'an full of reminder, you will certainly be resurrected," and similar to it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, meaning in pride and refusal to accept the truth, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," the arrogance takes him to sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206]. In the language of the Arabs, "ʿizzah" means domination and subjugation. It is said: "Whoever is mighty plunders," meaning whoever overcomes despoils. From it comes: ﴿And he has overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23], meaning he overcame me. Jarir said:

*He prevails over the road with his shoulders,*
*as the dispossessed gambler prevails over the arrows.* [The line describes a camel that prevails over the other camels in keeping to the road, and urges onward, and compares his eagerness to keep the road and to press on with the eagerness of this dispossessed gambler to cast the arrows, hoping to recover some of what he lost of his wealth. The *khalī'* is the one stripped of his property and crushed.]

He meant: prevails. "And opposition" means in showing disagreement and opposition. It comes from *shiqq* (a side), as if this is on one side and that on the other. This was explained fully before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 2, p. 143, second edition.]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many a generation We destroyed before them﴾, meaning peoples who were more powerful than these. "Kam" is a word of multiplicity. ﴿And they cried out﴾, meaning with pleas for help and repentance. Calling out (al-nidā') is raising the voice, and from it comes the report: "Throw it to Bilal, for he is louder in voice than you," meaning higher.

﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Hasan said: They called out in repentance, but it was not the time for repentance, nor a time when deeds would benefit. Al-Nahhas said: This is his explanation of the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "but it was no time for escape." As for Israel, he narrated from Abu Ishaq, from al-Taymi, from Ibn 'Abbas: "But it was no time for escape." He said: It was not a time for leaping (nazw), which is a kind of running, nor for fleeing. He said: They were all restrained. Al-Kalbi said: When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others: "Manāṣ," meaning: "You must flee and be defeated." But when the punishment came upon them, they said: "Manāṣ." Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Qushayri said: On this view, the estimate is: "They called out, 'Manāṣ,'" and it was omitted because the rest of the speech indicates it, meaning: it is not the time for what you call out for. There is some arbitrariness in this, since it is far-fetched to say that every generation that perished used to say "Manāṣ" when compelled.

It is also said: The meaning of "But it was no time for escape" is: "But it was no time for deliverance," and it is in the accusative by the negation of *lā* (lā li-khalāṣ) acting on it. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this, because on this view there is no meaning for the wāw in "But it was no time for escape." Al-Jurjani said: That is, "they called out when there was no escape," meaning an hour in which there is no refuge and no escape. Since he placed "lā" first and delayed "ḥīn," that required the wāw, just as the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) requires it when it is made an inceptive sentence and a predicate. Like your saying: "Zayd came riding," but when you make it an inceptive sentence and predicate, it requires the wāw, as in "Zayd came to me while he was riding." So "ḥīn" is an adverb of time for His words: "they called out."

"Manāṣ" means retreat, flight, and deliverance. That is, they called out seeking deliverance at a time when there was no deliverance for them. Al-Farra' said:

*Is it from the mention of Layla, when she removed herself from you, and you became hesitant?* [The full line: *"...fa-taqṣuru ʿanhā khaṭwatan wa-tabūṣu,"* meaning: "so you fall short of her by a step and go forward."]

It is said: *nāṣa ʿan qirnihi yanūṣu nawṣan wa-manāṣan*, meaning he fled and turned aside. Al-Nahhas said: It is also said: *nāṣa yanūṣu* when he advanced. I say: On this view, it is among the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād). *Al-nawṣ* is the wild donkey. *Istanāṣa* means he drew back, as al-Jawhari said.

The grammarians have discussed "But it was no time" and the pause upon it, and Abu 'Ubayda al-Qasim ibn Sallam expanded on this in his book on the readings, but nearly all he said is rejected, except for a few points. Sibawayh said: "Lāt" is made similar to "laysa," and its subject is a pronoun, meaning: "Our times are not a time of escape." He related that some of the Arabs put it in the nominative, saying: "wa-lātu ḥīnin manāṣ" [and it is no time for escape]. He related that the nominative is rare, and the predicate is omitted just as the subject was omitted in the accusative, meaning: "and it is no time for escape for us." The pause upon it, according to Sibawayh and al-Farra', is on "lāt" with a tāʾ, then one begins with "ḥīna manāṣ." This is the view of Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan said: The view is as Sibawayh said, because it is made similar to "laysa," so just as one says "laysat," one says "lāt."

The pause upon it according to al-Kisa'i is with a hā': "lāh." This is the view of al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid. Ali ibn Sulayman related from him that the proof for this is that a hā' was added to it for the feminization of the word, just as one says "thumma" (then) becoming "thummah," and "rubba" (perhaps) becoming "rubbah." Al-Qushayri said: It is also said "thumat" meaning "thumma," and "rubbat" meaning "rubba," so they added a hā' to "lā," saying "lāh," just as they said with "thummah," at the pause it becomes a tāʾ.

Al-Tha'labi said: The people of the language said: "Lāt ḥīn" are two words with fatḥa, as if they were one word, and it is only "lā" with a tāʾ added to it, like "rubba" and "rubbat," and "thumma" and "thummat." Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i said:

*They sought our reconciliation, but it was not the time,*
*and we answered that it is not a time for survival.*

Another said:

*Remembrance of the love of Layla has come to you, no longer in time,*
*and old age has come and cut off the companion.*

Among the Arabs there are those who put "lāt" in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*So you will surely recognize people subdued,*
*and you will surely regret, and it is no time for regret.*

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash held that the *ta'* in *wa-lāta ḥīn* is separate from *ḥīn*, and they said its meaning is *wa-laysat* ("and it was not"). The same is written in the new and old *maṣāḥif* (copies of the Qur'an), with the *ta'* separated from *ḥīn*. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna also held this view.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: "In my view, the pause (*waqf*) on this word is on *wa-lā*, and the new start is *taḥīna manāṣ*, so the *ta'* is joined to *ḥīn*." Some said: "*Lāt*," then he starts again with "*ḥīna manāṣ*."

Al-Mahdawi said: Abu 'Ubayd mentioned that the *ta'* in the *muṣḥaf* is joined to *ḥīn*, and this is an error according to the grammarians (*naḥwiyyīn*), and it contradicts the view of the exegetes (*mufassirīn*). Abu 'Ubayd's argument was that he said: "We have not found the Arabs adding this *ta'* except to *ḥīn*, *awān* and *al-ān*." He cited Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

*"Al-'ātifūna taḥīna mā min 'āṭifin… wa-l-muṭ'imūna zamāna Ibn al-Muṭ'am"*

He cited Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i:

*"Ṭalabū ṣulḥanā wa-lāta awāni… fa-ajabnā an laysa ḥīna baqā'"*

So he added the *ta'* to *awān*. Abu 'Ubayd said: From their adding the *ta'* to *al-ān* is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both). A man asked him about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), and he mentioned his virtues, then said: "Take it with you *talān*." Likewise is the saying of the poet [[It is Jamil ibn Ma'mar, and after it:
"Indeed the best of those who connect in purity… is the one who meets his beloved wherever they are."]]:

*"Nuwallī qabla nay'i dārī Jumānā… wa-ṣilīnā kamā zaʿamti talānā"*

Abu 'Ubayd said: Despite all of this, I deliberately looked at what is called the *imam* (the *muṣḥaf* of 'Uthman), and I found the *ta'* joined with *ḥīn*, written as *taḥīn*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: As for the first verse which Abu Wajza cited, the scholars of language transmitted it in four ways, all of them contrary to what he cited. In one of them there are two interpretations. Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) transmitted it as:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta mā min 'āṭif"*

The second transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta ḥīna ta'āṭufin"*

The third transmission was narrated by Ibn Kaysan:

*"Al-'āṭifūnah ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

He made it a *hā'* in pause and a *tā'* in continuous speech (*idrāj*), and he claimed that it is to show the vowel (*li-bayān al-ḥaraka*), being likened to the feminine *hā'*. The fourth transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūnahu ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

In this transmission there are two interpretations. One of them, which is the view of Isma'il ibn Ishaq, is that the *hā'* is in the accusative position, as you say: *al-ḍāribūna Zaydan*; when you use a pronoun you say: *al-ḍāribūhu*. Sibawayh permitted in poetry *al-ḍāribūnahu*, so Isma'il gave the feminine form following Sibawayh's permission of its like. The other interpretation is that the *hā'* is to show the vowel, as you say: *marra bina al-muslimūnah* in pause, and then in continuous speech it is treated as it is in pause, as the people of Madina recited: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ ۝ هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28–29] ("My wealth has not benefited me; my authority has perished from me").

As for the second verse, there is no proof in it, because it is paused upon as: *(wa-lāta awān)*. However, there is a difficulty in it, because it is transmitted as *(wa-lāta awānin)* with the genitive (*khafḍ*), whereas what follows *lāta* is only nominative or accusative. Although it has been transmitted from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he recited *"wa-lāti ḥīnin manāṣ"* with a kasra on the *tā'* of *lāt* and on the *nūn* of *ḥīn*, the established reading from him is that he recited *"wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ"*, so he built *lāt* on the kasra and put *ḥīn* in the accusative. As for *(wa-lāta awān)*, it has two interpretations. Al-Akhfash said: there is a hidden element in it, meaning *wa-lāta ḥīna awān*.

Al-Nahhas said: This view is clearly wrong. The other interpretation, from Abu Ishaq, said: its meaning is *wa-lāta awānunā*, so he deleted the *muḍāf ilayh* (the noun annexed to), and therefore it was required that it not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), and he gave it a kasra because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited it as *(wa-lāta awānu)* with a *ḍamma*.

As for the third verse, it is a later (*muwallad*) verse whose composer is unknown, and no proof can be established by it. Moreover, Muhammad ibn Yazid transmitted it as *(kamā zaʿamti al-āna)*. Others said: the meaning is *kamā zaʿamti anti al-āna*, so he dropped the *hamza* from *anti* and the *nūn*. As for his argument from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, when he mentioned the virtues of 'Uthman to the man and said to him: "Take it with you *talān* to your companions," there is no proof in it, because the transmitter only narrates this according to its meaning. The evidence for this is that Mujahid narrates this hadith from Ibn 'Umar and says in it: "Go and strive your utmost." Another narrated it: "Take it with you *al-āna*." As for his argument that he found it in the *Imam* as *"taḥīnu"*, there is no proof in it, because the meaning of *Imam* is that it is the leader of the *maṣāḥif*; if it opposes them, then it is not their *imam*, and in all the *maṣāḥif* it is *"wa-lāta"*. So if there were nothing in this but this argument, it would be convincing.

The plural of *manāṣ* is *manāwiṣ*.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Sad is Meccan according to all scholars, and it has eighty-six verses. It is also said to have eighty-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ (1) ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ (2) ﴿How many a generation We destroyed before them, and they cried out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ (3)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Sad﴾. The common reading is "Ṣ" with the dal pronounced with a jazm (sukun) because of pausing, since it is one of the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijā'), like "Alif Lam Mim" and "Alif Lam Mim Ra." Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn 'Asim read "Ṣādi" with a kasra on the dal and without tanwin.

For this reading there are two views (madhhabān).

The first is that it derives from ṣādā, yuṣādī, meaning "to oppose" (ʿāraḍa). From it comes Allah's words: ﴿As for him who is rich, you attend to him eagerly﴾ [ʿAbasa: 6], meaning "you present yourself to him." Al-muṣādāh is opposition, and from it comes al-ṣadā, which is the echo that answers the voice in empty places. So the meaning is: "Oppose the Qur'an with your deeds, answer it with them, act upon its commands, and refrain from what it forbids." Al-Nahhas said: This view is reported from al-Hasan, who explained his reading with it as a sound transmission (riwāyah ṣaḥīḥah). It is also reported from him that the meaning is: "Recite it and present yourself to its recitation."

The second view is that the dal is kasra because of the meeting of two sakin letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn).

Isa ibn 'Umar read "Ṣāda" with a fatḥa on the dal, like "Qāf" and "Nūn" with a fatḥa on their final letters. For this reading there are three views. The first is that it means "recite" (utlu). The second is that it was given a fatḥa because of the meeting of two sakin letters, and he preferred the fatḥa for assimilation (ittibā') and because it is the lightest of the vowels. The third is that it is in the accusative by way of an oath without a particle, like your saying: "Allah, I will certainly do it." It is also said that it is in the accusative by way of incitement (al-ighrā'). It is also said that the meaning is: Muhammad ﷺ won over the hearts of the creation and attracted them until they believed in him.

Ibn Abi Ishaq also read "Ṣādin" with a kasra on the dal and tanwin, on the basis that it is in the genitive by omission of the particle of oath. This is far-fetched, although Sibawayh permitted something similar. It may also be that it is treated like those words that do not take full inflection, such as sounds and other things.

Harun al-A'war and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read "Ṣādu," "Qāfu," and "Nūnu" with a ḍamma on their final letters, because it is the form known for indeclinability (binā') in most cases, as in mundhu, qaṭṭu, qablu and baʿdu. And when you make "Ṣ" the name of the surah, it is not declined (lam yanṣarif), just as when you name a feminine thing with a masculine name it is not declined, even if its letters are few.

Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah were asked about "Ṣ," and both said: "We do not know what it is."

Ikrima said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about "Ṣ," and he said: "Ṣ" was a sea in Mecca, and the Throne of the Merciful was upon it, when there was neither night nor day.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Ṣ" is a sea by which Allah will bring the dead to life between the two blasts.

Al-Dahhak said: Its meaning is "Allah has spoken truly" (ṣadaqa Allāh).

It is also reported from him that "Ṣ" is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names, may He be exalted.

Al-Suddi said, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas as well.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is the key to the names of Allah, the Eternal Refuge (Ṣamad), the Maker of created things (Ṣāni' al-maṣnū'āt), and the One true to His promise (Ṣādiq al-wa'd).

Qatada said: It is one of the names of the Merciful. It is also reported from him that it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

Mujahid said: It is the opening of the surah.

It is also said: It is among the things which Allah has kept to Himself in knowledge, and this is the meaning of the first view.

All of this has been mentioned before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 155, second or third edition.]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the Qur'an﴾. It is in the genitive by the oath particle wāw, and the wāw replaces the bāʾ. He swears by the Qur'an to draw attention to its great rank, for in it is the explanation of everything, a cure for what is in the breasts, and a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿Full of reminder﴾ is in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt), and the sign of its genitive is the yāʾ, since it is a defective noun (ism muʿtall), and its original form is dhawā on the pattern faʿala. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: The meaning of "full of reminder" is full of clarification (dhī al-bayān). Al-Dahhak said: full of honour, meaning whoever believes in it will have honour in both abodes, as Allah says: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10], meaning your honour. Also, the Qur'an is noble in itself because of its inimitability and because it contains what nothing else contains. It is also said: "Full of reminder" means that it contains mention of what is needed of the matters of religion. It is also said: it contains mention of the names of Allah and His glorification. It is also said: meaning full of admonition and remembrance.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and there are several views about it.

It is said that the answer to the oath is "Ṣ," because its meaning is "true" (ḥaqq), so it is the answer to the phrase "And the Qur'an," just as you say: "Truly, by Allah," "He descended, by Allah," "It is obligatory, by Allah." In this case, pausing on "And the Qur'an, full of reminder" is good (ḥasan), and pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is complete (tamām). Ibn al-Anbari said this, and al-Tha'labi transmitted its meaning from al-Farra'.

It is also said: the answer is "Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition," because "bal" (nay, but) negates something that came before and affirms something else. This was said by al-Qutabi, so it is as if he said: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition against accepting the truth and in enmity toward Muhammad ﷺ." Or it is: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder — the matter is not as they say, that you are a sorcerer and a liar, for they know you for truthfulness and trustworthiness; rather they are proud and refuse to accept the truth." This is like His words: ﴿Qāf. By the glorious Qur'an. Nay, but they wonder﴾ [Qāf: 1–2].

It is also said: the answer is ﴿How many a generation We destroyed﴾ [Qāf: 36], as if he said: "By the Qur'an, how many We destroyed," and when the particle "kam" came after, the lām was removed from it, like His words: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9], meaning "indeed he has succeeded." Al-Mahdawi said: This is the view of al-Farra'. Ibn al-Anbari said: On this view, pausing on "in arrogance and opposition" is not complete.

Al-Akhfash said: The answer to the oath is "Indeed all of them denied the Messengers, so My punishment was justified," and similar to it is His words: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 97], and His words: "By the heaven and the night-visitant," up to His words ﴿Indeed every soul...﴾ [al-Tariq: 1–4]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them, and the verses and stories are many.

Al-Kisa'i said: The answer to the oath is His words: ﴿Indeed that is true, the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is uglier than the first, because the speech is even longer between the oath and its answer.

It is also said that the answer is His words: ﴿Indeed this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54].

Qatada said: The answer is omitted, and its estimate is: "By the Qur'an full of reminder, you will certainly be resurrected," and similar to it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, meaning in pride and refusal to accept the truth, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," the arrogance takes him to sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206]. In the language of the Arabs, "ʿizzah" means domination and subjugation. It is said: "Whoever is mighty plunders," meaning whoever overcomes despoils. From it comes: ﴿And he has overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23], meaning he overcame me. Jarir said:

*He prevails over the road with his shoulders,*
*as the dispossessed gambler prevails over the arrows.* [The line describes a camel that prevails over the other camels in keeping to the road, and urges onward, and compares his eagerness to keep the road and to press on with the eagerness of this dispossessed gambler to cast the arrows, hoping to recover some of what he lost of his wealth. The *khalī'* is the one stripped of his property and crushed.]

He meant: prevails. "And opposition" means in showing disagreement and opposition. It comes from *shiqq* (a side), as if this is on one side and that on the other. This was explained fully before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 2, p. 143, second edition.]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many a generation We destroyed before them﴾, meaning peoples who were more powerful than these. "Kam" is a word of multiplicity. ﴿And they cried out﴾, meaning with pleas for help and repentance. Calling out (al-nidā') is raising the voice, and from it comes the report: "Throw it to Bilal, for he is louder in voice than you," meaning higher.

﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Hasan said: They called out in repentance, but it was not the time for repentance, nor a time when deeds would benefit. Al-Nahhas said: This is his explanation of the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "but it was no time for escape." As for Israel, he narrated from Abu Ishaq, from al-Taymi, from Ibn 'Abbas: "But it was no time for escape." He said: It was not a time for leaping (nazw), which is a kind of running, nor for fleeing. He said: They were all restrained. Al-Kalbi said: When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others: "Manāṣ," meaning: "You must flee and be defeated." But when the punishment came upon them, they said: "Manāṣ." Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿But it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Qushayri said: On this view, the estimate is: "They called out, 'Manāṣ,'" and it was omitted because the rest of the speech indicates it, meaning: it is not the time for what you call out for. There is some arbitrariness in this, since it is far-fetched to say that every generation that perished used to say "Manāṣ" when compelled.

It is also said: The meaning of "But it was no time for escape" is: "But it was no time for deliverance," and it is in the accusative by the negation of *lā* (lā li-khalāṣ) acting on it. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this, because on this view there is no meaning for the wāw in "But it was no time for escape." Al-Jurjani said: That is, "they called out when there was no escape," meaning an hour in which there is no refuge and no escape. Since he placed "lā" first and delayed "ḥīn," that required the wāw, just as the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) requires it when it is made an inceptive sentence and a predicate. Like your saying: "Zayd came riding," but when you make it an inceptive sentence and predicate, it requires the wāw, as in "Zayd came to me while he was riding." So "ḥīn" is an adverb of time for His words: "they called out."

"Manāṣ" means retreat, flight, and deliverance. That is, they called out seeking deliverance at a time when there was no deliverance for them. Al-Farra' said:

*Is it from the mention of Layla, when she removed herself from you, and you became hesitant?* [The full line: *"...fa-taqṣuru ʿanhā khaṭwatan wa-tabūṣu,"* meaning: "so you fall short of her by a step and go forward."]

It is said: *nāṣa ʿan qirnihi yanūṣu nawṣan wa-manāṣan*, meaning he fled and turned aside. Al-Nahhas said: It is also said: *nāṣa yanūṣu* when he advanced. I say: On this view, it is among the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād). *Al-nawṣ* is the wild donkey. *Istanāṣa* means he drew back, as al-Jawhari said.

The grammarians have discussed "But it was no time" and the pause upon it, and Abu 'Ubayda al-Qasim ibn Sallam expanded on this in his book on the readings, but nearly all he said is rejected, except for a few points. Sibawayh said: "Lāt" is made similar to "laysa," and its subject is a pronoun, meaning: "Our times are not a time of escape." He related that some of the Arabs put it in the nominative, saying: "wa-lātu ḥīnin manāṣ" [and it is no time for escape]. He related that the nominative is rare, and the predicate is omitted just as the subject was omitted in the accusative, meaning: "and it is no time for escape for us." The pause upon it, according to Sibawayh and al-Farra', is on "lāt" with a tāʾ, then one begins with "ḥīna manāṣ." This is the view of Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan said: The view is as Sibawayh said, because it is made similar to "laysa," so just as one says "laysat," one says "lāt."

The pause upon it according to al-Kisa'i is with a hā': "lāh." This is the view of al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid. Ali ibn Sulayman related from him that the proof for this is that a hā' was added to it for the feminization of the word, just as one says "thumma" (then) becoming "thummah," and "rubba" (perhaps) becoming "rubbah." Al-Qushayri said: It is also said "thumat" meaning "thumma," and "rubbat" meaning "rubba," so they added a hā' to "lā," saying "lāh," just as they said with "thummah," at the pause it becomes a tāʾ.

Al-Tha'labi said: The people of the language said: "Lāt ḥīn" are two words with fatḥa, as if they were one word, and it is only "lā" with a tāʾ added to it, like "rubba" and "rubbat," and "thumma" and "thummat." Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i said:

*They sought our reconciliation, but it was not the time,*
*and we answered that it is not a time for survival.*

Another said:

*Remembrance of the love of Layla has come to you, no longer in time,*
*and old age has come and cut off the companion.*

Among the Arabs there are those who put "lāt" in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*So you will surely recognize people subdued,*
*and you will surely regret, and it is no time for regret.*

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash held that the *ta'* in *wa-lāta ḥīn* is separate from *ḥīn*, and they said its meaning is *wa-laysat* ("and it was not"). The same is written in the new and old *maṣāḥif* (copies of the Qur'an), with the *ta'* separated from *ḥīn*. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna also held this view.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: "In my view, the pause (*waqf*) on this word is on *wa-lā*, and the new start is *taḥīna manāṣ*, so the *ta'* is joined to *ḥīn*." Some said: "*Lāt*," then he starts again with "*ḥīna manāṣ*."

Al-Mahdawi said: Abu 'Ubayd mentioned that the *ta'* in the *muṣḥaf* is joined to *ḥīn*, and this is an error according to the grammarians (*naḥwiyyīn*), and it contradicts the view of the exegetes (*mufassirīn*). Abu 'Ubayd's argument was that he said: "We have not found the Arabs adding this *ta'* except to *ḥīn*, *awān* and *al-ān*." He cited Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

*"Al-'ātifūna taḥīna mā min 'āṭifin… wa-l-muṭ'imūna zamāna Ibn al-Muṭ'am"*

He cited Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i:

*"Ṭalabū ṣulḥanā wa-lāta awāni… fa-ajabnā an laysa ḥīna baqā'"*

So he added the *ta'* to *awān*. Abu 'Ubayd said: From their adding the *ta'* to *al-ān* is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both). A man asked him about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), and he mentioned his virtues, then said: "Take it with you *talān*." Likewise is the saying of the poet [[It is Jamil ibn Ma'mar, and after it:
"Indeed the best of those who connect in purity… is the one who meets his beloved wherever they are."]]:

*"Nuwallī qabla nay'i dārī Jumānā… wa-ṣilīnā kamā zaʿamti talānā"*

Abu 'Ubayd said: Despite all of this, I deliberately looked at what is called the *imam* (the *muṣḥaf* of 'Uthman), and I found the *ta'* joined with *ḥīn*, written as *taḥīn*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: As for the first verse which Abu Wajza cited, the scholars of language transmitted it in four ways, all of them contrary to what he cited. In one of them there are two interpretations. Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) transmitted it as:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta mā min 'āṭif"*

The second transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūna wa-lāta ḥīna ta'āṭufin"*

The third transmission was narrated by Ibn Kaysan:

*"Al-'āṭifūnah ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

He made it a *hā'* in pause and a *tā'* in continuous speech (*idrāj*), and he claimed that it is to show the vowel (*li-bayān al-ḥaraka*), being likened to the feminine *hā'*. The fourth transmission:

*"Al-'āṭifūnahu ḥīna mā min 'āṭif"*

In this transmission there are two interpretations. One of them, which is the view of Isma'il ibn Ishaq, is that the *hā'* is in the accusative position, as you say: *al-ḍāribūna Zaydan*; when you use a pronoun you say: *al-ḍāribūhu*. Sibawayh permitted in poetry *al-ḍāribūnahu*, so Isma'il gave the feminine form following Sibawayh's permission of its like. The other interpretation is that the *hā'* is to show the vowel, as you say: *marra bina al-muslimūnah* in pause, and then in continuous speech it is treated as it is in pause, as the people of Madina recited: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ ۝ هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28–29] ("My wealth has not benefited me; my authority has perished from me").

As for the second verse, there is no proof in it, because it is paused upon as: *(wa-lāta awān)*. However, there is a difficulty in it, because it is transmitted as *(wa-lāta awānin)* with the genitive (*khafḍ*), whereas what follows *lāta* is only nominative or accusative. Although it has been transmitted from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he recited *"wa-lāti ḥīnin manāṣ"* with a kasra on the *tā'* of *lāt* and on the *nūn* of *ḥīn*, the established reading from him is that he recited *"wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ"*, so he built *lāt* on the kasra and put *ḥīn* in the accusative. As for *(wa-lāta awān)*, it has two interpretations. Al-Akhfash said: there is a hidden element in it, meaning *wa-lāta ḥīna awān*.

Al-Nahhas said: This view is clearly wrong. The other interpretation, from Abu Ishaq, said: its meaning is *wa-lāta awānunā*, so he deleted the *muḍāf ilayh* (the noun annexed to), and therefore it was required that it not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), and he gave it a kasra because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited it as *(wa-lāta awānu)* with a *ḍamma*.

As for the third verse, it is a later (*muwallad*) verse whose composer is unknown, and no proof can be established by it. Moreover, Muhammad ibn Yazid transmitted it as *(kamā zaʿamti al-āna)*. Others said: the meaning is *kamā zaʿamti anti al-āna*, so he dropped the *hamza* from *anti* and the *nūn*. As for his argument from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, when he mentioned the virtues of 'Uthman to the man and said to him: "Take it with you *talān* to your companions," there is no proof in it, because the transmitter only narrates this according to its meaning. The evidence for this is that Mujahid narrates this hadith from Ibn 'Umar and says in it: "Go and strive your utmost." Another narrated it: "Take it with you *al-āna*." As for his argument that he found it in the *Imam* as *"taḥīnu"*, there is no proof in it, because the meaning of *Imam* is that it is the leader of the *maṣāḥif*; if it opposes them, then it is not their *imam*, and in all the *maṣāḥif* it is *"wa-lāta"*. So if there were nothing in this but this argument, it would be convincing.

The plural of *manāṣ* is *manāwiṣ*.

The Qur'anic verse ﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾. "Anna" is in the accusative position, and the meaning is "because a warner had come to them." It has been said that this is connected to His words, "in arrogance and dissension," meaning: "they are in arrogance and dissension, and they wondered." His words, "How many generations We destroyed before them," are a parenthetical interjection. It has also been said: No, rather this is the beginning of a new statement, meaning: "and from their ignorance, they openly expressed amazement that a warner had come to them from among themselves." ﴿So the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer"﴾, meaning he brings speech that is embellished, by which people are deceived. It has also been said that by his sorcery he separates the father from his son and the man from his wife. ﴿"A liar"﴾, meaning in his claim to prophethood.

The Qur'anic verse ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ has two objects, meaning he made the gods into one god. ﴿"Indeed, this is a thing astonishing"﴾, meaning wondrous. al-Sulami recited "ʿujjāb" with a shaddah. "ʿAjāb," "ʿujāb," and "ʿajab" are the same in meaning. Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) distinguished between "ʿajīb" and "ʿujāb," saying: "ʿAjīb" is the one who causes amazement, while "ʿujāb" is one that has exceeded the limit of amazement, just as "ṭawīl" is one that has length, and "ṭiwāl" is one that has exceeded the limit of length. Al-Jawhari said: "ʿAjīb" is a matter at which one marvels, and likewise "ʿujāb" with a damma, while "ʿujjāb" with a shaddah is more intense than it, and likewise "u'jūbah." Muqatil said: "ʿujjāb" is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a tribe.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Talib fell ill, so the Quraysh came to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came too. At the head of Abu Talib was a seat for a man, so Abu Jahl stood up in order to prevent him. He said: They complained about him to Abu Talib, and he said: "O nephew, what do you want from your people?" He said: "O uncle, I only want from them one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them and the non-Arabs ('Ajam) will pay them the jizya (poll tax)." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "There is no god but Allah." They said: ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God?"﴾ He said: So the Qur'an was revealed concerning them: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder. Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and dissension﴾, until ﴿"This is nothing but a fabrication"﴾. Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it with the same meaning, and said: This is a hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and authentic).

It has also been said: When 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) embraced Islam, his conversion was difficult for the Quraysh, so they gathered before Abu Talib and said: "Judge between us and your nephew." So Abu Talib sent for the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O nephew, these are your people. They ask you for fairness [[In the manuscripts of the source: "they ask you what is harmful." In Abu al-Mas'ud: "they ask you for fairness and equity." In al-Baydawi, as in al-Kashshaf: "they ask you the question." Al-Shihab commented on it, saying: "The apparent reading is that it is a distortion, and that it is al-sawa', meaning justice, as occurs in other tafsirs."]], so do not incline entirely toward your people." He said: "And what do they ask of me?" They said: "Leave us alone, and leave off mentioning our gods, and we will leave you and your God." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will you give me one word, and by it you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs will submit to you?" Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, your father! We will give it to you and ten like it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Say: There is no god but Allah." They recoiled from that and stood up, saying: ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a thing astonishing"﴾, meaning how can one God be sufficient for all of creation? So Allah revealed these verses concerning them, up to His words: ﴿"The people of Noah denied before them"﴾ [Ṣād: 12].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 6–11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: "Walk on, and be steadfast in your gods."﴾ "Al-mala'" (the chiefs, the notables). "Al-intilaq" is going away quickly. That is, these disbelievers departed from the presence of the Messenger, peace be upon him, saying to one another, "Walk on" (amshu), meaning: go on in what you were upon and do not enter into his religion. "And be steadfast in your gods." It has also been said that this refers to their walking to Abu Talib during his illness, as has already been mentioned. In the narration of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, they were Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Shaybah and Utbah, the sons of Rabi'ah ibn Abd Shams, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and Abu Mu'it. They came to Abu Talib and said: "You are our chief, and you have been fair to us in ourselves. So relieve us of the matter of your brother's son and the foolish ones with him, for they have abandoned our gods and attacked our religion." Abu Talib sent for the Prophet ﷺ and said to him: "Your people are calling you to what is equitable and fair." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am only calling them to one word." Abu Jahl said: "And ten." He said: "You say: There is no god but Allah." They stood up and said: "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing" (the verses). "Walk on" (an amshu): "an" is in the position of a accusative, and the meaning is "that walk on." It has also been said that "an" here means "i.e." (ay), so that: "And the chiefs among them went forth," i.e., "Walk on." This is an explanation of their departure, not that they spoke with this wording. It has also been said: the meaning is that the notables among them went forth and said to the common people: "Walk on and be steadfast in your gods," i.e., in the worship of your gods. ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾, i.e., this which Muhammad, peace be upon him, has brought is something intended against the people of the earth, to remove blessings from some people and to bring them down upon others. It has also been said that "Indeed, this is a thing that is intended" is a word of warning: that is, Muhammad only intends by what he says that they submit to him, so that he may rise above us and we become his followers, and he will then rule over us as he wishes. So beware of obeying him. Muqatil said: When Umar embraced Islam and Islam was strengthened by him, this grieved the Quraysh, and they said: "Indeed, the Islam of Umar, at the height of Islam's strength, is a thing that is intended."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾

Ibn Abbas, al-Qurazi, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: they meant the religion of Jesus, the Christian religion, which is the last of the religions, and the Christians associate a god with Allah. Mujahid and Qatadah also said: they meant the religion of Quraysh. Al-Hasan said: "We have not heard that this would occur at the end of time." It has also been said: that is, "We have not heard from the People of the Book that Muhammad is a true messenger." ﴿It is nothing but fabrication﴾, i.e., a lie and invention, according to Ibn Abbas and others. It is said: "khalaqa" and "ikhtalaqa," meaning he invented, and Allah, mighty and majestic, created creation from this, i.e., He originated them without a model.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of denial, and "the Reminder" here means the Qur'an. They denied that he should be singled out for revelation from among them. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, i.e., about My revelation, which is the Qur'an. That is, they knew that you had always been truthful among them, but they doubted whether what I sent down to you was from Me or not. ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, i.e., they were only deceived by the prolonged respite. Had they tasted My punishment for their polytheism, doubt would have departed from them, and they would not have said that. But faith would not benefit them at that time. "Lamma" here means "lam" (not yet), and "ma" is an extra particle, as in His saying: ﴿After a little while﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40], and His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ [an-Nisa': 155].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ It has been said: "Or do they have this, so that they may prevent Muhammad, peace be upon him, from that with which Allah, mighty and majestic, has favored him, namely prophethood?" "Am" (or) may come with the meaning of reproach when the speech is connected to what precedes it, as in His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ [as-Sajdah: 1–3]. It has also been said that His saying: "Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord" is connected to His saying: ﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ [Sad: 4]. So the meaning is that Allah, mighty and majestic, sends whom He wills, because the treasuries of the heavens and the earth belong to Him. ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?﴾ That is, if they claim that, ﴿then let them ascend by the means﴾, i.e., let them climb to the heavens, and let them prevent the angels from bringing down revelation upon Muhammad. It is said: "raqiya yarqa" and "irtaqa" when one ascends. And "raqa yarqi raqyan," like "rama yarmi ramyan," from "ruqyah" (incantation). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "The asbab (means) are finer than hair and harder than iron, but they are not seen." The sabab in the language is everything by which one reaches the desired object, whether a rope or otherwise. It has also been said: the asbab are the gates of the heavens through which the angels descend, as said by Mujahid and Qatadah. Zuhayr said:

"And if he were to seek the asbab of the heaven by a ladder..."
[[Half-line: "Whoever shuns the causes of death, they will reach him."]]

It has also been said: the asbab are the heavens themselves, i.e., let them ascend heaven by heaven. Al-Suddi said: "fi al-asbab" means in excellence and religion. It has been said: i.e., let them rise in the means of power, if they think that these prevent. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu 'Ubaydah. It has also been said: the asbab are ropes, meaning if they find a rope or a means by which they can ascend to the sky, then let them climb, and this is a command of reproach and of incapacitation. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 12–14:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾. He mentioned them as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and as solace for him. That is, these from your people, O Muhammad, are a host of the earlier confederates who banded together against their prophets, and they were stronger than these, yet they were destroyed. Allah the Exalted used the feminine form for "the people" (al-qawm), and the scholars of Arabic grammar (ahl al-'Arabiyyah) differed on this in two opinions. The first: it is permissible to use both the masculine and the feminine with it. The second: its wording is masculine and it is not permissible to make it feminine, except when the meaning falls upon the clan (al-'ashirah) and the tribe (al-qabilah), in which case the ruling of the implied meaning prevails in the wording as a reminder of it, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54–55], and He did not say "dhakarahā," because the pronoun implied in it was masculine, so He made it masculine, even though the wording required the feminine.

He described Pharaoh as "Dhu al-Awtad" (the Lord of the Stakes). Its interpretation has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is "the one of firmly built structures." Al-Dahhak said: he had many buildings, and buildings are called awtad (stakes). It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and 'Ata' that he had stakes, ropes and playgrounds on which games were played for him. And it is related from al-Dahhak also: "the one of strength and force." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: he used to torture people with stakes, and when he became angry with someone he would stretch him out on his back between four stakes driven into the ground, and send upon him scorpions and snakes until he died. It was also said: he would crucify the tormented person between four pillars, each extremity of his to a pillar, with an iron stake driven into it, and leave him until he died. It was said: "Dhu al-Awtad" means "the one of many armies," so the armies were called stakes, because they strengthen his affair just as the stake strengthens the tent. Ibn Qutaybah said: the Arabs say, "they are in firmly established might (fi 'izz thabit al-awtad)," meaning lasting and strong. The origin of this is that a tent of hair (bayt min buyut al-sha'r) stands and stays up only by stakes. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"And they lived in it in the most pleasant of lives, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firmly fixed."

The singular of awtad is watid, with a kasrah, and with a fathah is another dialect. Al-Asma'i said: it is said watid and wati, as one says shaghl shaghil. And he recited [the line of Abu Muhammad al-Fuq'asi; the pronoun in "laqat" refers to the camels]:

"She met upon the water a judhayl (stump) and a wati (stake), and it did not fail her in its promises."

He said: he likened the man to a jidhl (stump).

"And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket (al-Aykah)": al-Aykah means the thicket. Its mention has already passed in [al-Shu'ara' (Chapter 26)] [see vol. 13, p. 134 and following, first or second edition].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "Laykah" with a fathah on the lam and the ta' without hamz. The rest read it with hamz and kasrah on the ta'. This has already been discussed.

"Those are the confederates (al-Ahzab)": that is, they are the ones described as having strength and numbers, as when you say, "So-and-so is the man."

"Not one of them but denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due" (in meaning, "in ma kull"): that is, the punishment descended upon them because of that denial. Ya'qub kept the yā' in "'adhabi" and "'iqabi" in both states, while the rest omitted it in both states.

The parallel to this verse is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the one who believed said: O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the confederates, like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Ghafir: 30–31], thus He named these nations "confederates."

It was said: "Dhu al-Awtad" means "the one of many armies," so the armies were called stakes, because they strengthen his affair just as the stake strengthens the tent. Ibn Qutaybah said: the Arabs say, "they are in firmly established might (fi 'izz thabit al-awtad)," meaning lasting and strong. The origin of this is that a tent of hair (bayt min buyut al-sha'r) stands and stays up only by stakes. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"And they lived in it in the most pleasant of lives, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firmly fixed."

The singular of awtad is watid, with a kasrah, and with a fathah is another dialect. Al-Asma'i said: it is said watid and wati, as one says shaghl shaghil. And he recited [the line of Abu Muhammad al-Fuq'asi; the pronoun in "laqat" refers to the camels]:

"She met upon the water a judhayl (stump) and a wati (stake), and it did not fail her in its promises."

He said: he likened the man to a jidhl (stump).

"And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket (al-Aykah)": al-Aykah means the thicket. Its mention has already passed in [al-Shu'ara' (Chapter 26)] [see vol. 13, p. 134 and following, first or second edition].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "Laykah" with a fathah on the lam and the ta' without hamz. The rest read it with hamz and kasrah on the ta'. This has already been discussed.

"Those are the confederates (al-Ahzab)": that is, they are the ones described as having strength and numbers, as when you say, "So-and-so is the man."

"Not one of them but denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due" (in meaning, "in ma kull"): that is, the punishment descended upon them because of that denial. Ya'qub kept the yā' in "'adhabi" and "'iqabi" in both states, while the rest omitted it in both states.

The parallel to this verse is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the one who believed said: O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the confederates, like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Ghafir: 30–31], thus He named these nations "confederates."

The Qur'an says: ﴿And these [Meccan disbelievers] await only a single cry﴾. "Yanzuru" here means "yantadhiru" (awaits), as in His saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. "These" refers to the disbelievers of Makkah. "A single cry" means the blast of the Resurrection, that is, they await nothing after they were struck at Badr except the cry of the Resurrection.

It has also been said: their living now await only the cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet, as He says: ﴿They await only a single cry that will seize them while they are disputing. So they will not be able to make any bequest﴾ [Ya-Sin: 49-50]. This is an announcement of the nearness of the Resurrection and of death.

It has also been said: the meaning is that the disbelievers at the end of this community, who adhere to the religion of those (earlier disbelievers), await only a single cry, which is the blast.

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: No cry has ever occurred in the sky except as an anger from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, against the people of the earth.

﴿Has no fawaq﴾: that is, no repetition (tardid), according to Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: it has no return (ruju'). Qatadah said: it has no second instance (mathniyyah). As-Suddi said: it has no recovery (ifaqah).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "mā lahā min fuwāq" with a ḍammah on the fa'. The rest of the readers (al-Baqun) read it with a fatḥah. [Qira'ah: a canonical mode of reciting the Qur'an.]

Al-Jawhari said: al-fawaq and al-fuwaq are the time between the two milkings, because the she-camel is milked, then left for a short while so that the young camel may suckle her, to make her milk flow again, and then she is milked. It is said: "He did not stay with him except for a fawaq." And in the hadith: "The visit (to the sick) is the length of a fawaq of a she-camel."

The saying of Allah, ﴿mā lahā min fawāq﴾, is read with fatḥah and ḍammah, meaning: it has no respite, rest or recovery.

Al-fiqah with kasrah is the name of the milk that gathers between the two milkings. The waw became a yā' because the letter before it is kasrah. Al-A'sha, describing a cow, said:

*"Until, when fiqah has gathered in her udder, and she came to suckle, the side of the soul, if it had suckled."*

The plural is fiqa, then afwaq, like shibr and ashbar, then afawiq. Ibn Hammam as-Salouli said:

*"They denounced the world to us while they themselves suckle it, and its afawiq, until the ta'l does not make it flow for them."* [The verse is about the scholars of this world who denounce it while greedily clinging to it. Ta'l is an extra teat on the udder of a she-camel, cow or sheep, which does not produce milk; he mentioned it for emphasis.]

Al-afawiq also means the water that gathers in the clouds, so that it rains hour after hour. And the she-camel "afaqat ifaqah," meaning the fiqah gathered in her udder; so she is mufiq and mufiqah, according to Abu 'Amr. The plural is mafawiq.

Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: "min fawāq" with a fatḥah on the fa' means a rest in which they do not recover, as the sick person or the one who has fainted recovers. And "min fuwāq" with a ḍammah on the fa' means from waiting. It has already been mentioned that both have the same meaning, which is the time between the two milkings.

I say: the intended meaning is that it is continuous, with no interruption in it. Abu Hurayrah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us while we were in a group of his companions, the hadith. In it: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commands Israfil to blow the first blast. He says: 'Blow the blast of terror.' The people of the heavens and the people of the earth are terrified, except whom Allah wills. He commands him, and he prolongs it, makes it continuous, and extends it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿These await only a single cry, which has no fawaq﴾."

He mentioned the hadith. Ali ibn Ma'bad and others narrated it, as we mentioned in the book al-Tadhkirah.

The Qur'an says: ﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our qitt before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ Mujahid said: our punishment. Likewise Qatadah said: our share of the punishment. Al-Hasan said: our share of Paradise, so that we may enjoy it in this world. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said it.

It is well known in the language that qitt is used for a share and also for a written document of a reward. Al-Farra' said: qitt in the speech of the Arabs means a portion and a share, and from this the cheque (sakk) is called qitt. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Kisa'i said: qitt is a written document of rewards, and its plural is quṭūṭ. Al-A'sha said:

*"Nor the king al-Nu'man, on the day I met him, and by his grace he gives the quṭūṭ and rewards."*

He means documents of rewards. It is also narrated as "bi-ummatihi" instead of "bi-ghibtatihi," meaning by his grace and his noble state. "Yafiq" means "yuslih" (he sets right). It is also said that the plural of qitt is qittah, and in few cases uqut and aqtat. Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

As-Suddi said: they asked that their dwellings in Paradise be shown to them, so that they would know the reality of what they are promised. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: the meaning is: hasten for us our provisions. It was also said: the meaning is: hasten for us what suffices us, from their saying "qaṭni," meaning "it suffices me." It was also said: they said this in haste for their books, which they will be given in their right hands or behind their backs when the Qur'an is recited to them about it. This is the saying of Allah: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19], and ﴿As for him who is given his record behind his back﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 10].

The origin of qitt is qatt, which means cutting, and from it comes qatta al-qalam (he cut the pen). So qatt is a name for a piece cut from something, like qism and qass. It was then applied to a share, a document and provision, because it is cut off from others. However, in the sense of a document it is more commonly used and stronger in its literal meaning. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*"A people for whom is the courtyard of Iraq, and what is collected to them, and the qitt and the pen."*

"Before the Day of Reckoning" means before the Day of Resurrection, in this world, if the matter is as Muhammad says. All this was said by them in mockery.
