Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾. He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to be patient when they mocked him. And this [verse] is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾. When He mentioned the reports about the disbelievers, their opposition, and their rebuke by the destruction of the generations before them, He commanded His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to be patient over their harm, and consoled him with everything previously mentioned. Then He began to mention Dawud and the stories of the prophets, so that he might find solace in the patience of those among them who were patient, and so that he would know that in the Hereafter he has multiples of what Dawud and the other prophets were given. It was also said: the meaning is, be patient over their saying, and recount to them the tales of the prophets, so that they serve as proof of the soundness of your prophethood. "Dha al-Ayd" means possessor of strength in worship. He would fast one day and break his fast the next, and that is the most intense and the most excellent fast. He would pray half the night, he would not flee when he met the enemy, and he was strong in calling to Allah, may He be exalted. His saying "Our servant" is a display of his honor through this attribution. It is said: al-ayd and al-add, just as you say al-ayb and al-aab. A poet said:

"He did not call out, so now I call out"

From this comes "rajul ayyid," meaning a strong man. And "ta'ayyada al-shay'" means it became strong. A poet said:

When the bow is strung by the ayyid... and he shoots and strikes the kidneys and the fat

He means: when Allah strings the bow that is in the clouds, He shoots the kidneys of the camels and fattens them with fat, meaning through the plants that grow from the rain.

﴿Indeed he was oft-returning (awwab)﴾. Al-Dahhak said: meaning repentant (tawwab). According to others: whenever he remembered his sin or it occurred to his mind, he sought forgiveness for it, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times in a day and night." It is said "aba yaubu" when he returned, as [[It is Ubayd ibn al-Abras.]] said:

"Every absent one returns, but the one absent by death does not return."

So Dawud was constantly returning to obedience to Allah and His pleasure in every matter, and so he is worthy to be followed.

This passage contains four issues.

**First issue:** Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him﴾. "Yusabbihna" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Allah mentions what He gave him as a proof and a miracle, which is the glorification of the mountains with him. Muqatil said: When Dawud remembered Allah, the mountains remembered Him with him, and he understood the glorification of the mountains. Ibn Abbas said: "Yusabbihna" means "they pray" (yuṣallīna). This would be a miracle only if people saw it and recognized it. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Dawud was given such a beautiful voice that the mountains resounded beautifully with it, and the birds listened attentively to its beauty and sang along with him. This is the glorification of the mountains and the birds. It was also said: Allah subjected them to move along with him, and that is their glorification, because it indicates the exaltation of Allah above resemblance to created beings. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Saba' [see vol. 14, p. 265 and following, first or second edition] and in Surat Subhan, at the words of Allah: ﴿And there is nothing except that it glorifies [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra: 44] [see vol. 10, p. 268, first or second edition]. The correct view among the opinions is that this is glorification by speech. And Allah knows best.

"Bil-'ashiyyi wal-ishraq" (in the evening and at sunrise). Al-Ishraq also means the whitening of the sun after its rising. It is said: the sun "sharaqat" when it rose, and "ashraqat" when it shone. Dawud used to glorify [Allah] after his prayer at sunrise and at sunset.

**Second issue:** It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: I used to pass over this verse, "in the evening and at sunrise," and I did not know what it meant, until Umm Hani told me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon her, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer, and said: "O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq." Ikrimah said that Ibn Abbas said: I had some doubt about the forenoon prayer until I found it in the Qur'an: "They glorify [Him] in the evening and at sunrise." Ikrimah said: Ibn Abbas did not used to pray the forenoon prayer, and then he prayed it afterward. It is also narrated that Ka'b al-Ahbar said to Ibn Abbas: I find in the books of Allah a prayer after the rising of the sun, which is the prayer of the penitents (al-awwabin). Ibn Abbas said: And I will show you it in the Qur'an, in the story of Dawud: "They glorify [Him] in the evening and at sunrise."

**Third issue:** The forenoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā) is a recommended voluntary prayer (nāfila). In the morning it corresponds to the afternoon prayer in the evening. It should not be prayed until the sun has risen brightly, its haze has lifted, and it shines with its light, just as the afternoon prayer is not prayed when the sun has turned yellow. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, it is narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The prayer of the penitents is when the young camels' feet burn from the heat." "Al-fiṣāl" and "al-fiṣlān" are plurals of "faṣīl," which is the camel that has been weaned from suckling. "Al-ramḍā'" is the intense heat on the ground. The young camels are singled out here because they are the ones whose feet burn before the intensity of the heat ends, which burns their mothers, due to the little endurance they have. This happens at forenoon or a little after, which is the middle period between the sunrise and its decline. Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said this. Some people hasten to pray it earlier, to get to their work, and thus lose their deed, because they pray it at a time that is forbidden, and they bring a deed that is against them, not for them.

**Fourth issue:** At-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays twelve rak'ahs of the forenoon prayer, Allah will build for him a palace of gold in Paradise." He said: It is a gharib hadith. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every joint of one of you has a charity to be given every morning. Every tasbih is a charity, every tahlil is a charity, every takbir is a charity, enjoining good is a charity, and forbidding evil is a charity. And two rak'ahs that he prays of the forenoon prayer will suffice for all of that." In at-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever preserves the even [rak'ahs] of the forenoon prayer, his sins will be forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea." Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "My close friend (khalil) enjoined three things upon me, which I will not abandon until I die: fasting three days each month, the forenoon prayer, and sleeping on witr." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. Muslim said: "And two rak'ahs of the forenoon prayer." He transmitted it from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', just as al-Bukhari transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. All of this indicates that the minimum of the forenoon prayer is two rak'ahs and its maximum is twelve. And Allah knows best.

The root of "al-sulamā" (with a dammah on the sīn) is the bones of the fingers, the palms, and the feet. Then it was used for all the bones of the body and its joints. It is narrated from the hadith of ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every human being among the children of Adam has been created with three hundred and sixty joints. Whoever says 'Allahu akbar,' praises Allah, says 'La ilaha illa Allah,' glorifies Allah, seeks Allah's forgiveness, and removes a stone, or a thorn, or a bone from the path of people, and enjoins good or forbids evil, [doing so] equal to the number of those three hundred and sixty joints, then he walks that day having distanced himself from the Fire." Abu Tawba said: Sometimes he said, "yumsi" (he walks in the evening) instead. Thus Muslim transmitted it. His saying "and two rak'ahs suffice from that" means that two rak'ahs suffice from these charities for these limbs. This is because prayer is an act involving all the limbs of the body, so when one prays, every limb has performed its duty that is incumbent upon it originally. And Allah knows best.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the birds gathered﴾** is in the same construction as "the mountains" (in the preceding verse). Al-Farra' said: "If it were read *wal-tayru mahshuratun* (with *al-tayru* in the nominative), it would be permissible, because the verb has not been made explicit." Ibn 'Abbas said: "When Dawud (peace be upon him) glorified Allah, the mountains would echo his glorification, and the birds would gather to him and glorify Allah along with him. Their gathering to him is their *hashr* (being gathered)." So the meaning is: "We subjected the birds, gathered to him, so that they would glorify Allah with him." It was also said: the meaning is "We subjected the wind so that it would gather the birds to him, so that they would glorify (Allah) with him," or "We commanded the angels to gather the birds." **﴿Each one was returning to Him﴾**, that is, to Dawud, **"constantly returning"** meaning obedient: they would come to him and glorify (Allah) with him. It was also said that the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾**, meaning We made it strong until it became firm. It was said: through awe, and by casting dread of him into hearts. It was said: through a large number of soldiers. It was said: through support and victory. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Indeed, a large army gathered around one who is not aided and not supported does not benefit him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Dawud was the most powerful of the kings of the earth in authority. Every night, more than thirty thousand men guarded his *mihrab* (prayer niche). When morning came, it was said: 'Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you.'" *Al-malik* (king) is an expression for a great quantity of kingship. A man may have some dominion, but he is not called a king until this becomes abundant. If a man owns a house and a wife, he is not a king until he has a servant who spares him the burden of managing the benefits he needs for his human necessities. This meaning has already been discussed in *Bara'ah* [[See vol. 8 p. 171, first or second edition.]], and the reality of kingship has been fully treated in *al-Naml*.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾.** On this there are two issues.

*The first:* Allah's words **"wisdom"** mean prophethood, according to al-Suddi. Mujahid said: justice. Abu al-'Aliyah said: knowledge of the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Qatadah said: the Sunnah. Shurayh said: knowledge and jurisprudence. As for **"decisive speech,"** Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Qatadah said: it means the decisive judgment in legal rulings. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the clarification of speech. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is "the proof is upon the claimant and the oath is upon the one who denies." Shurayh, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah also said this. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and al-Sha'bi also said: it is the phrase *amma ba'd* (as for what follows), and he was the first to say it. It was also said: "decisive speech" is clear explanation that separates truth from falsehood. It was said: it is conciseness, by making a great meaning contained in few words. The meanings of these sayings are close to one another, and the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, encompasses them, because the basis of judgment in legal decisions rests on it, apart from the saying of Abu Musa.

*The second:* The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the knowledge of judgment (*'ilm al-qada'*), by your Lord, it is a distinct kind of knowledge and a specific, emphasized part of it, separate from knowing the rulings and discernment of the lawful and the unlawful. In the hadith: "'Ali is the best judge among you, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal is the most knowledgeable of you about the lawful and the unlawful." A man may be expert in the rulings on actions and aware of what is lawful and unlawful, yet not be capable of deciding a case. It is related that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to Yemen, some people dug a pit for a lion. The lion fell into it, and people crowded around the pit. A man fell into it and grabbed another, the other grabbed another, until they were four, and the lion wounded them in it and they died. The people took up weapons, and there was almost fighting between them. He said: I came to them and said: "Will you kill two hundred men for the sake of four people? Come, let me judge between you with a ruling. If you accept it, it is the judgment between you; if you refuse, bring the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he has more right to judge." He gave the first a quarter of the blood money, the second a third of the blood money, the third half the blood money, and the fourth the full blood money, and he placed the blood money (*diyat*) upon the tribes of those who dug the pit, divided among the four tribes. Some of them were angered and some were pleased. Then they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and recounted the story to him. He said: "I will judge between you." Someone said: "'Ali has already judged between us." They informed him of what 'Ali had decided, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The judgment is as 'Ali has judged." In another narration: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ upheld the judgment of 'Ali.

Similarly, it is related in *al-Ma'rifah bi-al-Qada'* (Knowledge of Judgeship) that a man came to Abu Hanifa and said: "Ibn Abi Layla, who was judge in Kufa, flogged a mad woman who said to a man, 'O son of the two adulterers!' He flogged her two *hadds* (prescribed punishments) in the mosque while she was standing." He said: "He erred in six respects." Ibn al-'Arabi said: What Abu Hanifa said is grasped immediately only by scholars through observation, but the judgment of 'Ali cannot be grasped by the ignorant, nor reached except by one who is persistently devoted to rulings after long practice.

The reality of 'Ali's judgment is this: these four who were killed by mistake through the pushing of those present at the pit. Therefore they are owed blood money from those present, in terms of error. However, the first was killed by being pushed and was himself the killer of three by pulling. So he is owed the blood money for what was done to him, and upon him is three-quarters of the blood money for the three he killed. As for the second, he is owed a third of the blood money, and upon him are two-thirds for the two he killed by pulling. As for the third, he is owed half the blood money and upon him is half, because he killed one by pulling, so the shares were balanced (*al-muhasasah*), and the tribes (*al-'awaqil*) bore this calculation after the retaliation (*qisas*) that applied to it. This is one of the most wonderful deductions. As for Abu Hanifa, he considered the related meanings and saw them as six. The first: the madwoman has no *hadd* upon her, because madness removes legal responsibility. This is when the slander occurred during madness. But if she alternates between madness and sanity, she is punished for slander committed during her sane state. The second: her saying "O son of the two adulterers!" For that, he flogged her two *hadds*, one for each father. Abu Hanifa criticized him on the basis of his school's view that the *hadd* for slander is absorbed (into one punishment), because for him it is a right of Allah, the Exalted, like the *hadd* for wine-drinking and fornication. Al-Shafi'i and Malik, however, hold that the *hadd* for slander is a right of the human being, so it is multiplied according to the number of persons slandered. The third: he flogged her without the demand of the one slandered, and it is not permitted, by consensus of the community, to enforce the *hadd* for slander except after the demand for its enforcement by the one who says it is a right of Allah, and by the one who says it is a right of the human being. On this basis the argument is made by those who hold it is a right of the human being, for if it were a right of Allah, it would not depend on a demand, like the *hadd* for fornication. The fourth: he joined the two *hadds* together, but whoever is liable to two *hadds* is not subjected to them consecutively. Rather he is flogged for one of them, then left until the wound heals, [[Addition from Ibn al-'Arabi.]] "or until the one flogged recovers," and then the other *hadd* is enforced. The fifth: he punished her while she was standing, but a woman is only to be punished while seated and covered. Some people said: in a basket (*zinbil*). The sixth: he enforced the *hadd* in the mosque, and *hadds* are not enforced in mosques by consensus. As for judging in a mosque and *ta'zir* (discretionary punishment) there, there is disagreement.

The judge said: This is the *fasl al-khitab* (decisive speech) and the knowledge of judgment, to which reference was made through the interpretations of the hadith that is narrated: "'Ali is the best judge among you." As for those who said that it is conciseness, that belongs to the Arabs and not to non-Arabs, and to Muhammad ﷺ above the Arabs, and this was explained by his saying: "I have been given *jawami' al-kalim* (comprehensive words)." As for those who said that it is the phrase *amma ba'd*, the Prophet ﷺ would say in his sermon: "Amma ba'd." It is narrated that the first person to say it in the pre-Islamic era was Sahban ibn Wa'il, who was the first to believe in resurrection, the first to lean on a staff, and he lived one hundred and eighty years. Even if it were established that Dawud, peace be upon him, said it, it would not have been in Arabic in this arrangement, but in his own tongue. And Allah knows best.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the birds gathered﴾** is in the same construction as "the mountains" (in the preceding verse). Al-Farra' said: "If it were read *wal-tayru mahshuratun* (with *al-tayru* in the nominative), it would be permissible, because the verb has not been made explicit." Ibn 'Abbas said: "When Dawud (peace be upon him) glorified Allah, the mountains would echo his glorification, and the birds would gather to him and glorify Allah along with him. Their gathering to him is their *hashr* (being gathered)." So the meaning is: "We subjected the birds, gathered to him, so that they would glorify Allah with him." It was also said: the meaning is "We subjected the wind so that it would gather the birds to him, so that they would glorify (Allah) with him," or "We commanded the angels to gather the birds." **﴿Each one was returning to Him﴾**, that is, to Dawud, **"constantly returning"** meaning obedient: they would come to him and glorify (Allah) with him. It was also said that the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾**, meaning We made it strong until it became firm. It was said: through awe, and by casting dread of him into hearts. It was said: through a large number of soldiers. It was said: through support and victory. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Indeed, a large army gathered around one who is not aided and not supported does not benefit him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Dawud was the most powerful of the kings of the earth in authority. Every night, more than thirty thousand men guarded his *mihrab* (prayer niche). When morning came, it was said: 'Return, for the Prophet of Allah is pleased with you.'" *Al-malik* (king) is an expression for a great quantity of kingship. A man may have some dominion, but he is not called a king until this becomes abundant. If a man owns a house and a wife, he is not a king until he has a servant who spares him the burden of managing the benefits he needs for his human necessities. This meaning has already been discussed in *Bara'ah* [[See vol. 8 p. 171, first or second edition.]], and the reality of kingship has been fully treated in *al-Naml*.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾.** On this there are two issues.

*The first:* Allah's words **"wisdom"** mean prophethood, according to al-Suddi. Mujahid said: justice. Abu al-'Aliyah said: knowledge of the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Qatadah said: the Sunnah. Shurayh said: knowledge and jurisprudence. As for **"decisive speech,"** Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Qatadah said: it means the decisive judgment in legal rulings. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the clarification of speech. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is "the proof is upon the claimant and the oath is upon the one who denies." Shurayh, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah also said this. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and al-Sha'bi also said: it is the phrase *amma ba'd* (as for what follows), and he was the first to say it. It was also said: "decisive speech" is clear explanation that separates truth from falsehood. It was said: it is conciseness, by making a great meaning contained in few words. The meanings of these sayings are close to one another, and the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, encompasses them, because the basis of judgment in legal decisions rests on it, apart from the saying of Abu Musa.

There are twenty-four issues in it.

The first: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the wall of the prayer niche?﴾ "Al-khasm" (the litigant, the adversary) applies to one, to two, and to a group, because its origin is the verbal noun (masdar). The poet said:

*And adversaries, angry, shaking their beards,*
*like the shaking of well-bred Arab horses, when they toss their manes.*

Al-Nahhas said: There is no disagreement among the people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) that what is meant here are two angels. It was said that "they climbed over" (tasawwaru) is in the plural even though they were two, treating them as "al-khasm," since it is in the form of a collective noun and is equivalent to it, like "al-rakb" (riders) and "al-sahb" (companions). Its implied sense is: for the two there were two parties to the dispute, and for the group there were parties to the dispute.

The meaning of "they climbed over the prayer niche" (tasawwaru al-mihrab) is that they came to it from the top of its wall. It is said: "tasawwara al-ha'it" (he scaled the wall), meaning he climbed it. "Al-sur" is the city wall, and it is without a hamza. Likewise "al-suwar" is the plural of "surah" (a stage, a rank), like "busrah" and "busr." It is every station of a building. From it comes the term "surat al-Qur'an" (a chapter of the Qur'an), because it is one station after another, separated from the next. The explanation of this has already passed in the introduction of this book (see vol. 1, p. 65 and following, second or third edition). The saying of al-Nabighah:

*Did you not see that God has given you a "surah" (a rank),*
*and you see every king below it wavering?*

means nobility and station. As for "al-su'r" with a hamza, it is the remainder of food in the vessel. Ibn al-Arabi said: "al-su'r" is a feast, and it is Persian. In a hadith: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of the Confederates: "Indeed Jabir has prepared a feast (sawr) for you, so welcome to you (fa-haiyahla bikum)." "Al-mihrab" here means the upper chamber, because they climbed over it into it, as Yahya ibn Sallam said. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the front of the assembly, and from it comes the "mihrab" of the mosque. The discussion of this has passed in several places.¹

﴿When they entered upon Dawud⦆ "jā'at" (came) is repeated as "idh" (when) twice, because they are two verbs. Al-Farra' claimed that one of them has the meaning of "lamma" (when). Another view is that the second "idh" together with what follows it is an explanation of what came before it. It was said: they were two humans, as al-Naqqash said. It was said: they were two angels. A group said so. A group specified them and said: they were Jibril and Mika'il. It was also said: they were two angels in the form of two humans, whom God sent to him on the day of his worship. The guards prevented them from entering, so they climbed over the prayer niche onto him. He did not notice while he was in prayer until they were sitting before him. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the prayer niche?⦆ That is, they ascended and descended over it from above the prayer niche, as Sufyan al-Thawri and others said.

The reason for this, as Ibn 'Abbas related, is that Dawud, peace be upon him, said to himself: "If I am tested, I will be steadfast." It was said to him: "You will indeed be tested, and you will know the day on which you will be tested, so take your precaution." So he took the Zabur (Psalms) and entered the prayer niche and forbade anyone from entering upon him. While he was reading the Zabur, a bird came, the most beautiful of birds, and began to hop before him. He intended to take it with his hand, and it lured him until it fell into the window of the prayer niche. He approached it to take it, and it flew off. He looked out to see it and saw a woman bathing. When she saw him, she covered her body with her hair. Al-Suddi said: so it fell into his heart. Ibn 'Abbas said: her husband was away fighting in the way of God, and he was Uriya ibn Hanan. Dawud wrote to the commander of the fighters that he should place her husband among the bearers of the Ark. The bearers of the Ark would either be granted victory by God or be killed. So he sent him forward among them, and he was killed. When her waiting period had ended, Dawud proposed to her. She stipulated that if she bore a boy he would be the caliph after him. She wrote a document to him with this condition and called fifty men of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him. His soul was not at rest until she bore Sulayman, who grew up. And the two angels climbed over, and what happened between them was what God related in His Book. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others. But it is not sound. Ibn al-Arabi said: "It is the most plausible of what has been related on this matter."²

*We prefer the judgment of reason in every doubt,*
