It is nonsense and fabrication, as al-Baydawi said, and it impugns the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them. Abu Hayyan spoke well and excellently when he said: "It is known with certainty that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sins; they cannot fall into any of them, because if we allowed any of that for them, the sacred laws would be nullified, and we could not trust anything they say God revealed to them. What God related in His Book passes as He intended, and what the storytellers (qussas) relate that disparages the station of prophethood we discard." We, as the poet said:

*We prefer the judgment of reason in every doubt,*
*and if the transmitters of reports prefer, they are storytellers.*

Al-Raqqashi's narration is rejected by verification. Al-Qurtubi will later quote from al-Nahhas on page 175 what supports what we have cited.

I say: al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated it with the same meaning as a hadith traced to the Prophet, in *Nawadir al-Usul*, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, who heard Anas ibn Malik say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When the Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) looked at the woman and desired her, he sent a military expedition for the Children of Israel and instructed the commander of the expedition, saying: 'When the enemy is present, bring forward so-and-so,' and he named him. He said: So he brought him forward before the Ark (al-tabut). He said: That Ark, in that era, was used to seek victory. Whoever was sent forward before the Ark would not return until he was killed or the army fighting against it was defeated. So he was sent forward and was killed, and the woman's husband was slain. Then the two angels came down to Dawud and related the story to him."

Sa'id narrated from Qatadah: He wrote to her husband while they were besieging the city of Amman, the city of Balqa' [the note: "the city of Balqa'," meaning the capital of al-Balqa'], to take hold of the door-ring, and in that was death. So he advanced and was killed.

Al-Tha'labi said: Some scholars said: Allah tested Dawud with the sin only because he once wished of his Lord the rank of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and asked Him to test him as He had tested them and to give him what He had given them. Dawud had divided time into three days: a day in which he judged among the people, a day in which he was alone worshipping his Lord, and a day in which he was alone with his wives and his affairs. He found in the books he read the virtue of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. He said: "O Lord, all goodness has gone to my forefathers." Allah revealed to him: "They were tried with trials that no one else was tried with, and they endured them. Ibrahim was tried with Nimrod, with the fire, and with the sacrifice of his son. Ishaq was tried with being sacrificed. Ya'qub was tried with grief over Yusuf and the loss of his sight. You have not been tried with any of that." Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "Then test me with the like of what You tested them with, and give me the like of what You gave them." Allah revealed to him: "You will be tried in such-and-such month, on Friday." When that day came, he entered his mihrab, closed its door, and began to pray, reciting the Zabur (Psalms). While he was in that state, Satan appeared to him in the form of a golden dove, with every beautiful colour in it. It stood between his feet, and he reached out his hand to take it and give it to a young son of his. It flew off, not far, and did not give up hope of him, so he stretched toward it to take it, and it moved away. He followed it, and it flew until it landed in a window (kuwwa). He went to take it, and it flew off, and Dawud looked up, rising after it to send someone to catch it. Then he saw a woman in a garden by the edge of a pool, bathing. This was related by al-Kalbi. Al-Suddi said: She was bathing naked on her roof. He saw the most beautiful of women in form. She saw his shadow, so she shook out her hair and it covered her body, which increased his admiration for her.

Her husband was Uriyya ibn Hanan, who was on a campaign with Ayyub ibn Surya, the son of Dawud's sister. Dawud wrote to Ayyub: "Send Uriyya to such-and-such a place and put him before the Ark." Whoever was put before the Ark was not permitted to turn back behind it until Allah granted victory or he was martyred. So he sent him forward, and victory was granted, and he wrote to Dawud informing him of it. Al-Kalbi said: Uriyya was the Sword of Allah on His earth in the time of Dawud. Whenever he struck a blow and said "Allahu akbar," Jibril would say "Allahu akbar" on his right and Mika'il on his left, and the angels of the heavens would say "Allahu akbar" in response to his takbir, until it reached the Throne, and the angels of the Throne would say "Allahu akbar" in response to his takbir. He said: The swords of Allah were three: Kalib ibn Yufuna in the time of Musa, Uriyya in the time of Dawud, and Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When Ayyub wrote to Dawud informing him that Allah had granted victory through Uriyya, Dawud wrote to him: "Send him on such-and-such expedition and put him before the Ark." Allah granted victory through him, but he was killed in the third (expedition) as a martyr. Dawud then married that woman when her waiting period (iddah) ended. She is the mother of Sulayman ibn Dawud.

It was also said: The cause of Dawud's (peace be upon him) testing was that his soul told him he could endure a whole day without committing any sin. Al-Hasan said: Dawud divided time into four parts: a part for his wives, a part for worship, a part for the Children of Israel, who would discuss with him and whom he would discuss with, and whom he would make weep and who would make him weep, and a day for judgment. They debated whether a person could pass a day without committing a sin. Dawud concealed in himself that he could do that. So he closed the door on himself on the day of his worship, ordered that no one enter upon him, and devoted himself to reciting the Zabur. A golden dove fell before him, and he mentioned what has preceded. Our scholars said: In this there is evidence, and this is the second issue: that a judge is not obliged to sit for the people every day, and that a person may not abandon intercourse with his wives even if he is occupied with worship. This matter has already been discussed in (the commentary on) *al-Nisa'*. Ka'b judged this in the time of Umar, in his presence, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abdullah ibn Umar: "Your wife has a right over you," and the hadith continues.

Al-Hasan and also Mujahid said: When Dawud (peace be upon him) became ruler, he said to the Children of Israel: "By Allah, I will be just among you," and he did not say "if Allah wills," so he was tested with this.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Dawud was greatly devoted to worship, so he became impressed with his deed and said: "Is there anyone on earth who does deeds like mine?" [Allah sent Jibril to him (in the old manuscripts: "Allah revealed to him")], and said: "Allah the Exalted says to you: You are impressed with your worship, and self-admiration consumes worship as fire consumes firewood. If you become impressed again, I will leave you to yourself." He said: "O Lord, leave me to myself for a year." He said: "That is a lot." He said: "Then a month." He said: "That is a lot." He said: "Then a day." He said: "That is a lot." He said: "O Lord, then leave me to myself for an hour." He said: "Then do as you wish with it." So he appointed guards, wore wool, entered the mihrab, and placed the Zabur before him. While he was in his worship, the bird landed before him, and what happened with the woman happened.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: Dawud said one day: "O Lord, there is not a day but that one of the family of Dawud is fasting for You, and not a night but that one of the family of Dawud is standing in prayer for You." Allah revealed to him: "O Dawud, is that from you or from Me? By My might, I will leave you to yourself." He said: "O Lord, pardon me." He said: "I will leave you to yourself for a year." He said: "No, by Your might." He said: "Then a month." He said: "No, by Your might." He said: "Then a week." He said: "No, by Your might." He said: "Then a day." He said: "No, by Your might." He said: "Then an hour." He said: "No, by Your might." He said: "Then a moment." Satan said to him: "And what is the value of a moment?" He said: "Leave me to myself for a moment." So Allah left him to himself for a moment. It was said to him: "It will be on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such a time." When that day came, he devoted it to worship and appointed guards around his place. It was said: four thousand. It was also said: thirty thousand, or thirty-three thousand. He was alone in worship of his Lord and spread out the Zabur before him, and the dove came and landed before him, and what happened with the woman in that moment happened.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent the two angels to him after the birth of Sulayman, and they set forth to him the parable of the ewes. When he heard the parable he remembered his sin, so he fell down prostrate for forty nights, as will come.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He was frightened of them﴾, because they came to him at night at a time other than the time of the disputants entering. It was also said: because they entered upon him without his permission. And it was said: because they climbed over the mihrab to him and did not come to him through the door.

Ibn al-Arabi said: The mihrab of Dawud (peace be upon him) was so elevated and secure that no human could ascend to it by any device except by spending days or months building up to it, according to his capacity, with helpers in large numbers and various kinds of equipment. If we said that one reached it through the door of the mihrab, Allah would not have said, reporting this: ﴿they climbed over the mihrab﴾, since one does not say "tasawwara al-mihrab" (he climbed over the mihrab) or "al-ghurfa" (the upper chamber) of someone who ascends to it by its stairs and comes to it from below, unless it is used figuratively. When you see the window (kuwwa) through which it is said the two disputants entered, you will know with certainty that they were angels, because it is so high that only one from above can reach it. Al-Tha'labi said: It was also said that the two who climbed over were two brothers from the Children of Israel, sons of one father and one mother. When Dawud judged between them with a verdict, an angel said to him: "Why did you not judge that against yourself, O Dawud?" Al-Tha'labi said: The first (view) is better, that they were two angels who alerted Dawud to what he had done. I say: Most of the commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) hold this view.

If it is asked: How is it permissible for the two angels to say ﴿a dispute in which one of us has wronged the other﴾, when that is a lie, and angels are free of such things? The answer is that speech must include an implied element. It is as if they said: "Suppose we are two disputants, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth." On this interpretation their words ﴿This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾ are to be understood. Although it has the form of a report, the intent is to present it as a hypothetical so that Dawud would be alerted to what he had done, and Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: If it is asked: Why was Dawud frightened, when he was a prophet, whose soul was strengthened by prophethood, reassured by revelation, confident in the rank Allah had given him, in whose hands signs had appeared, and who was in the utmost position of courage? It is answered: That is the way of the prophets before him; they did not feel safe from being killed and harmed, and it was from these that they feared. Do you not see how Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) said: ﴿We fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress﴾, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Do not fear﴾? The messengers also said to Lut: ﴿Do not fear; we are messengers of your Lord; they will not reach you﴾, and so the two angels said here: ﴿Do not fear.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Allah sent to him two angels who came to dispute before him while he was in his mihrab, a parable that Allah struck for him and for Uriyya. He saw them standing over his head and said: "What brought you in to me?" They said: ﴿Do not fear. Two disputants, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth⦆ and so come to you to judge between us.

**Fifth:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is asked, how did (David) not order them to leave, since he knew their purpose, and why did he not discipline them when they had entered upon him without permission? The answer to this has four aspects.

First: we do not know the manner of his law (*shar'*) concerning the veil and permission. So the answer depends on those rulings. At the beginning of our law these rulings were left unspecified, until God Most High clarified them through explanation.

Second: if we applied the answer to the rulings of the veil, it would be possible that the alarm which came upon him distracted him from what was obligatory for him in that matter.

Third: he wanted to hear fully the statement for which they had entered, so that he would know the final outcome from it, and see whether their entering without permission could be excused, and whether they had an excuse for it or not. So the outcome was that what was revealed was a trial and a test, an example which God struck in the story, and a discipline that fell upon the claim to infallibility.

Fourth: it is possible that this took place in a mosque, and there is no permission needed in a mosque for anyone, since no one is restricted there.

I say: there is a fifth opinion, mentioned by al-Qushayri, that they said: "When the guardians of the chamber did not permit us, we reached entry by climbing over the wall, and we feared that the matter would escalate between us." So David accepted their excuse and gave ear to their words.

**Sixth:** God's words: ﴿two adversaries﴾. If it is asked: how did He say "two adversaries" when before this it says "when they climbed over the wall of the sanctuary"? It is answered: because two is itself a plural. Al-Khalil said: just as you say "we did" when you are two. Al-Kisa'i said: (it is) plural because it was a report, and when the report ended and the address came, the two spoke about themselves and said "two adversaries." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "we are two adversaries." Others said: the saying is elided, meaning: (they) say, "Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other." Al-Kisa'i said: if it had been "one of them has wronged the other," it would have been permissible.

Al-Mawardi said: they were two angels, and they were neither adversaries nor aggressors, and no lie could come from them. The construction of their speech is like your saying: "If two adversaries come to you and say, 'One of us has wronged the other...'"

It was also said: that is, "we are two groups of adversaries, one of us has wronged the other." On this view it is possible that the dispute was between two persons, each with a group behind him. It is also possible that each one of this group had a dispute with each one of the other group, so they came for the disputes, but two of them began. Thus David understood the story through mention of the ewe, and this made unnecessary any reference to the other disputes.

And "al-baghy" means transgression and going beyond what is due. It is said: "the wound transgressed (baghā)" when its pain became excessive and spread to what is shameful. From this comes "the woman transgressed (baghat)" when she committed indecency.

**Seventh:** God's words: ﴿So judge between us with truth and do not exceed (tushit)﴾, meaning: do not deviate. This was said by al-Suddi. Abu 'Ubayd related: "shatattu 'alayhi" (I exceeded against him), meaning I deviated. In the hadith of Tamim al-Dari: "Verily you are a shātt," meaning one who is unjust toward me in judgment. Qatada said: do not incline. Al-Akhfash said: do not be extravagant. It was also said: do not go to extremes. The meanings are close. The root of this is distance, from "shatta al-dar," meaning the house became distant; it is said: "shatta al-dar yashiṭṭu and yashuṭṭu, shaṭṭan and shuṭūṭan," it became distant. "Ashashṭa fi al-qadiyya" means he was unjust in the case; "Ashashṭa fi al-sawm" and "ishtaṭṭa" mean he went far (in the price); "ashashṭū fi ṭalabī" means they went to the utmost in seeking me. Abu 'Amr said: shaṭaṭ is exceeding the measure in everything. In the hadith: "She has the bride-price of her equal, without deficiency or excess (shaṭaṭ)," meaning without shortfall or increase. In the revelation: ﴿We would have said then an enormity (shaṭaṭan)﴾ [Al-Kahf: 14], meaning injustice in speech and distance from the truth. ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾ meaning: guide us to the straight way.

**Eighth:** God's words: ﴿Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes﴾. That is, the angel who spoke, about Uriyya, said: "Indeed, this is my brother," meaning one of my religion, and he pointed to the defendant. It was also said: "my brother" means "my companion." ﴿He has ninety-nine ewes﴾. Al-Hasan recited: "tis'un wa-tis'ūna na'jatan" with a fatha on the *ta'* in both, which is an anomalous dialect, and it is the correct reading of al-Hasan, said al-Nahhas.

The Arabs use the ewe and the sheep as a metaphor for a woman, because of her calmness, her weakness, and her meekness. She is also referred to by the cow, the ḥijra, and the she-camel, because all of these are ridden. Ibn 'Awn said:

*I am their father, three of them, and a fourth in the house, young,*
*and my ewe, five of them, I fulfil them,*
*and without a generous youth who feeds them,*
*they wind up, hungry, in the sand dunes,*
*and woe to the bread, woe to them from them.*

And 'Antara said:

*O ewe, what a hunter hunts, for the one to whom she is lawful,*
*and forbidden to me, and I wish she were not forbidden.*
*So I sent my slave-girl, and I said to her: go,*
*spy and learn her news for me.*
*She said: I saw an opening in the enemies,*
*and the ewe is available to whoever is wounded (or hunted).*
*Then it was as if she turned with the neck of a kid,*
*and a fawn of the gazelles, free, with a white blaze.*

And another (the poet is al-A'sha) said:

*I shot at the moment his eye was off his sheep,*
*and I hit the heart and the spleen of it.*

This is among the finest allusions, since he referred to women by sheep. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this, from the two angels, is an allusion and an alert, like their saying "Zayd struck 'Amr," though there was no striking nor sheep in actuality, as if he said: "We are two adversaries, this is our condition." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: the best thing said about this is that the meaning is: he says, "Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other," as a matter of inquiry, just as you say: "A man says to his wife such-and-such, what is obligatory upon him?"

I say: al-Muzani, the companion of al-Shafi'i, has interpreted this verse, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Ibn Shihab which the Muwatta' and others transmitted: "It is yours, O 'Abd ibn Zam'a," along these lines. Al-Muzani said: this hadith, in my view—and God knows best—may admit that the Prophet (ﷺ) answered the question and informed them of the ruling that this applies when there is a claimant of the marriage bed and a claimant of fornication. It is not that he accepted against 'Utba the statement of his brother Sa'd, nor against Zam'a the statement of his son that he was the child of fornication, because each of them reported about someone else. [[The editor's note: "that he is the child of fornication" is more fitting to the statement of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. See the hadith in "al-Muwatta'," vol. 6, p. 4, edition of Sultan 'Abd al-Hafiz.]] Muslims have unanimously agreed that the confession of one person about another is not accepted. God, the Glorified, has mentioned something similar in His Book, in the story of David and the angels, when they entered upon him and he was alarmed by them. They said: ﴿Do not fear; two adversaries﴾, though they were not two adversaries, nor did either of them have ninety-nine ewes; rather, they spoke to him in the form of a question, so that he would understand through it what they wished to make known. Thus it is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) judged in this story in the form of a question, even if no one supports me in this interpretation of the hadith; it is, in my view, sound. And God knows best.

**Ninth:** Al-Nahhas said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Indeed, this my brother had ninety-nine ewes, female." The "kāna" here is like the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And God was ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Al-Nisa: 96]. As for His saying "female," it is for emphasis, as one says: "He is a male man," and this is emphasis. It was also said: since it is said "these are a hundred ewes," even if there are a few males among them, it is permissible to say "female," to make known that there is no male among them. In the exegesis it is said: he had ninety-nine women. Ibn al-'Arabi said: if all of them were free, that is his law; if they were slave-women, that is our law. The apparent meaning is that the law of those before us was not restricted by a number, and the restriction is only in the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), because of the weakness of bodies and the shortness of lives. Al-Qushayri said: it is also possible to say that he did not have this exact number, but the intention is to strike an example, as you say: "If you came to me a hundred times I would not fulfil your need," meaning many times.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: some exegetes said David did not have a hundred wives; rather he mentioned the ninety-nine as an example. The meaning is: this (man) is rich in wives, and I am in need of them. This is corrupt for two reasons. First: turning away from the apparent meaning without evidence has no meaning, and there is no proof indicating that the law of those before us was limited in respect of women to what is in our law. Second: al-Bukhari and others narrated that Sulayman said: "Tonight I will go round to a hundred women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of God," and he forgot to say "if God wills." This is an explicit text.

**Tenth:** God's words: ﴿And I have one ewe﴾, meaning one woman. ﴿So he said: give her to me (akfilhā)﴾, meaning: step down for me from her until I take charge of her. Ibn 'Abbas said: give her to me. And from him: move over for me from her. This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud. Abu al-'Aliya said: join her to me until I take charge of her. Ibn Kaysan said: make her my portion and my share. ﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾, meaning he overcame me. al-Dahhak said: if he speaks, he is more eloquent than me, and if he fights, he is stronger than me. It is said: "'azzahu ya'uzzuhu" (with a damma on the 'ayn in the imperfect), meaning he overcame him. And in the proverb: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," meaning whoever prevails takes. The noun is *'izza*, which is strength and dominance. The poet said:

*A sandgrouse was caught in a snare, and it spent the night,*
*and the wing was caught as it struggled.*

Qur'an reciters Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayd ibn Umayr read: "wa-ʿazzanī fi l-khiṭāb" (and he overpowered me in the argument), meaning: he prevailed over me, from al-muʿazzah, which is al-mughalabah (overpowering); ʿazzahu means ghalabahu (he overcame him). Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The reason for the overpowering has been disputed. It is said: it means he overpowered me with his eloquence. It is also said: he overpowered me with his authority, because when he made his request I could not oppose him. In our country there was a governor called Sayr ibn Abi Bakr, and I spoke to him about asking someone on my behalf for a need. He said to me: "Do you not know that a ruler's request for a need is a usurpation of it?" I said: "As for when he is just, then no." I was amazed at his non-Arab speech (ʿujmah), his memorization of what he recited as an example, and his acumen, just as he was amazed at my answer to him and found it strange.

The Eleventh Issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his own ewes﴾. Al-Nahhas said: It is said that this was the sin of Dawud, peace be upon him, because he said "He has certainly wronged you" without verifying with evidence or an admission from the opponent whether this was so or not. This is one opinion, and its explanation will come later in the issue after this, and it is good, God willing. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: As for the statement of the scholars whose word cannot be rejected, among them Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas, they said: Dawud, peace be upon him, did no more than say to the man: "Transfer to me your wife." Abu Ja'far said: God, mighty and majestic, rebuked him for that and alerted him to it, and this is not among the major sins; whoever goes beyond this to something other than it is only bringing what is not authentically reported from a scholar, and he will bear a great sin for it. Thus he said in the book "I'rab al-Quran", and he said the same in his book "Ma'ani al-Quran". He (may God be pleased with him) said: Reports and narratives have come concerning the matter of Dawud, peace be upon him, and Uriyya; most of them are not authentic and their chains are not connected, and one should not venture to rely on such things except after knowing their authenticity. The most authentic report on this is that transmitted by Masruq from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: Dawud, peace be upon him, did no more than say "Transfer her to me" (akfilnīhā), that is, relinquish her to me. And al-Minhal reported from Said ibn Jubayr who said: Dawud (ﷺ) did no more than say: "Transfer her to me" (akfilnīhā), that is, move over from her and join her to me. Abu Ja'far said: This is the most distinguished of what has been reported on this matter, and the meaning according to it is that Dawud, peace be upon him, asked Uriyya to divorce his wife, just as a man asks another man to sell him his slave-girl. God, mighty and majestic, alerted him to this and rebuked him, since he was a prophet and had ninety-nine wives, and He disapproved of his occupying himself with worldly matters by seeking more of them. As for anything beyond this, one should not venture to speak of it. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: As for their claim that when she pleased him he ordered her husband to be sent forward to be killed in the way of God, this is absolutely false, for Dawud (ﷺ) would not have shed his blood for a purpose of his own. What happened was that Dawud said to one of his companions: "Transfer to me your wife," and he insisted on it, as a man asks another for a need with sincere desire, whether concerning a family matter or wealth. Sad ibn al-Rabiʿ said to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) established brotherhood between them: "I have two wives; I will relinquish the better of them to you." He said to him: "May God bless you in your family." What may be done at the outset may be requested, and the Qur'an does not state that this occurred, nor that he married her after the husband's marital bond with her had ended, nor that she bore Sulayman. From whom is this narrated and transmitted? And on whose transmission is reliance placed? No one among the trustworthy and firmly established narrators transmits it. As for Surat al-Ahzab, it contains a point indicating that the woman became Dawud's wife, namely His saying: ﴿There is no difficulty for the Prophet in what God has enjoined for him; this is God's way with those who passed away before﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38]. It means, in one opinion: the marriage of Dawud to the woman he had looked at, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh, except that Zaynab's marriage was not from a husband's request for separation; rather, he commanded him to keep his wife, whereas Dawud's marriage to the woman was through her husband's request for her separation. Thus this virtue belongs to Muhammad (ﷺ) over Dawud, added to his lofty virtues (ﷺ). However, it has been said that the meaning of "God's way with those who passed away before" is the marriage of prophets to women who gave themselves to them without a dowry. It was also said: by His saying "God's way with those who passed away before" He meant that the prophets, God's blessings be upon them, were assigned what they could carry out in marriage and other matters. This is the most sound opinion. The commentators have related that Dawud, peace be upon him, married one hundred women, and this is the explicit text of the Qur'an. It is also reported that Sulayman had three hundred wives and seven hundred slave-girls, and your Lord knows best. Al-Kiya al-Tabari mentioned in his "Ahkam" concerning God's saying, mighty and majestic: "And has there come to you the story of the disputants when they climbed over the sanctuary wall..." the verse: The scholars who hold that the prophets, peace be upon them, are free from major sins mentioned that Dawud, peace be upon him, had proceeded to propose to a woman who had been proposed to by another, called Uriyya; the people inclined to marry her to Dawud, desiring him and disinclined toward the first suitor, and Dawud was not aware of this, though he could have known it and turned away from this desire and from proposing to her; but he did not do so, since he was impressed by her, either through description or by seeing her unintentionally. Dawud, peace be upon him, had a large number of wives, while that suitor had no wife. So God, exalted is He, alerted him to what he had done through the two angels climbing over the wall and what they presented as an allegory in the manner of an indirect reproach, so that he would understand from it the place of rebuke and turn away from this course, and seek forgiveness from his Lord for this minor sin. The Twelfth Issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his own ewes﴾. In it is the giving of a legal ruling concerning the case after hearing from one of the two litigants, and before hearing from the other, according to the apparent sense of this statement. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is not permissible according to anyone, nor in any religion, and it is not possible for a human being. Rather, the sense of the speech is that one of the two litigants made a claim and the other conceded to the claim, and after that the ruling was given. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When two litigants sit before you, do not decide in favour of one of them until you have heard from the other." It was also said: Dawud did not decide for the other until his companion acknowledged that. It was also said: its meaning is "He has certainly wronged you, if it is so." God knows best which of these possibilities is intended. I say: al-Qushayri, al-Mawardi and others mentioned these two opinions. Al-Qushayri said: His saying "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe" without his having heard the opponent's speech is problematic, so it may be said: he only said this after reviewing the other litigant and after his admission. This has been reported, though its transmission is not established; it is known from contextual indicators. Or he meant: "He has certainly wronged you, if the matter is as you say," thereby silencing him with this and deferring him until he questioned his opponent. He said: It may be argued that among their law was reliance on the claimant's statement when the defendant remains silent, if no verbal denial appears from him. Al-Halimi Abu Abd Allah said in his book "Minhaj al-Din": Among what has come concerning thanks for an awaited blessing when it arrives, or when it was hidden and then appears, is prostration to God, mighty and majestic. He said: The basis for this is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: "And has there come to you the story of the disputants" up to His saying: "and a fine return." God, mighty and majestic, informed of Dawud, peace be upon him, that he heard the words of the complainant among the two litigants, and He did not report that he asked the other; He only related that he wronged him. The apparent sense of this is that he perceived in the speaker signs of weakness and oppression, so he took his matter as that of one wronged, as he said, and this led him not to question the opponent, so he said to him hastily: "He has certainly wronged you," although had he questioned him, he would have said: "I had a hundred ewes and he had nothing; this one he stole from me, and when I found it with him I told him to return it, and I did not tell him to transfer it to me; and he knew that I would bring him before you, so he came to you complaining before I could bring him, so that you would think he was the righteous one and I the wrongdoer." When Dawud spoke with what haste had driven him to, he knew that God, mighty and majestic, had left him to himself at that time, and that this was the trial we mentioned, and that this had come only from his own shortcoming. So he sought forgiveness from his Lord and fell down bowing to God, exalted is He, in thanks that He preserved him, in that he limited himself to wronging the one complained of and did not add to that any harshness, beating, or other such things befitting one who imagines in his heart that someone is a wrongdoer. God forgave him, then turned to him admonishing him, and said: ﴿O Dawud, We have made you a khalifah on earth, so judge between people with truth and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [Sad: 26]. Thus it became clear from what God, exalted is He, narrated of this admonition, which He directed to him after forgiveness, that his error was only a shortcoming in judgment and a hastiness in wronging one whose wrongdoing had not been established before him. Then it came from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Dawud prostrated in thanks, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in following him. Thus it is established that prostration of thanks is a sunnah transmitted by successive reports from the prophets, God's blessings be upon them. "Bi-suʾāli naʿjatika" means: by his asking of your ewe, so he attributed the verbal noun to the object and dropped the hāʾ from suʾāl; this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾ [Fussilat: 49], meaning: of his asking for good.

The Thirteenth Issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed many of the partners﴾. It is said: khalīṭ and khulaṭāʾ, but one does not say ṭawīl and ṭuwalāʾ, because of the heaviness of the movement on the wāw. In it there are two opinions: one of them is that they are companions. The second is that they are partners.

I say: applying the term "khulata'" (partners who mix their property) to partners in the strict sense is a stretch. The scholars differ over the definition of the khulata'. Most scholars said: it is when each person brings his own sheep and one shepherd gathers them, and they share the water-trough and the pen. Tawus and Ata' said: the khulata' are only the partners.

This contradicts the report, which is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Those who are separate are not to be combined, and those who are combined are not to be separated, for fear of the zakat. And when there are two partners, they shall settle between themselves equally." It is also reported as: "They shall reciprocate the surplus." There is no place for reciprocating a surplus among partners, so be aware of this.

The rulings on khultah (joint ownership) are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). Malik and his companions, and a group of scholars, do not hold that zakat [Addition required by the context.] is taken from a person whose share does not reach the amount on which zakat is obligatory. Al-Rabi', al-Layth, and a group of scholars, including al-Shafi'i, said: if the combined total reaches the amount on which zakat is obligatory, zakat is taken from them. Malik said: if the collector (al-musaddiq) acts on this, they shall reciprocate among themselves because of the disagreement on this matter, and it shall be like the ruling of a judge on which there is disagreement.

The fourteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, many of the partners wrong one another﴾, that is, they transgress and oppress. "Except those who believe and do righteous deeds" — for they do not wrong anyone. "And few are they" means the righteous, that is, "and few are they," so "mā" is superfluous (zā'idah). It was also said: it has the meaning of "alladhīna" (those who), and its implied sense is "and few are those who are...".

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) heard a man say in his supplication: "O Allah, make me among Your few servants." 'Umar said to him: "What is this supplication?" He said: "I intended the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.'" 'Umar said: "Every person is more knowledgeable than you, O 'Umar."

The fifteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And David thought that We had tried him﴾, that is, We tested him. "Thought" (ẓanna) means "was certain" (ayqana). Abu 'Amr and al-Farra' said: ẓanna has the meaning of ayqana, except that al-Farra' explained it by saying that it is not permissible, regarding what is directly observed, for ẓann to mean anything other than certainty.

The reading is "fatannāhu" with the nūn doubled and no doubling of the tā'. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) read "fattannāhu" with the tā' and nūn both doubled, for emphasis. Qatadah, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Ibn al-Sami'aqa read "fatanāhu" with both lightened. 'Ali ibn Nasr reported it from Abu 'Amr. The one meant is the two angels who entered upon David (peace be upon him).

The sixteenth issue: It is said that when David judged between them in the mosque, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, but David did not notice. They wished to make him aware, so they ascended to the sky opposite his face. David (peace be upon him) knew that Allah had tested him with this, and He alerted him to what He had tested him with.

I say: There is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates judging in the mosque except this verse, and those who said that judging in the mosque is permissible used it as evidence. If it were not permissible, as al-Shafi'i said, David would not have allowed them to do that, and he would not have said: "Go to the place of judgment." The Prophet (ﷺ) and the caliphs used to judge in the mosque. Malik said: judging in the mosque is an ancient practice, meaning in most matters. There is no harm in sitting in its courtyard, so that the weak, the polytheist, and the menstruating woman can reach him. He should not establish the hudud punishments there, but there is no harm in light discipline. Ashhab said: he may judge in his house and wherever he wishes.

The seventeenth issue: Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The caliphs used to judge personally, and the first to appoint a judge was Mu'awiyah. Malik said: judges should consult the scholars. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: a man should not be appointed a judge until he is knowledgeable in the reports of those who passed, consults people of opinion, is forbearing, and is free of blemish. He said: and he should be scrupulous. Malik said: he should be vigilant, very cautious of legal tricks, knowledgeable of conditions, and familiar with what he must know of Arabic, for rulings differ with the differences in expressions, claims, acknowledgments, testimonies, and conditions that include the rights of the one in whose favour the ruling is given. Before implementing the ruling in favour of the claimant, he should say: "Do you have any remaining proof?" If he says no, the ruling is applied against him, and no proof is accepted from him after the ruling is enforced, unless he brings something that has a valid basis or evidence. The rulings concerning judgment and judges, regarding what is due to them and what is incumbent upon them, are mentioned in other places.

The eighteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾. The exegetes differed over the sin for which he sought forgiveness, giving six opinions.

The first: that he looked at the woman until he was satisfied with her. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: his trial was only the glance. Abu Ishaq said: David did not intend to look at the woman, but he looked at her again, so the first look was for him and the second was against him.

The second: that he sent her husband out to the front lines in the carrying of the Ark.

The third: that he intended, if her husband died, to marry her.

The fourth: that Uriyya had proposed to that woman, and when he was absent, David proposed to her, and she was married to him because of his high status, and Uriyya was grieved by that. So Allah reproached David for not leaving her to her suitor. He already had ninety-nine wives.

The fifth: that he did not grieve over the killing of Uriyya, as he used to grieve over those of the army who perished, and then he married his wife, so Allah, Exalted is He, reproached him for that, because the sins of the prophets, though small, are great in the sight of Allah.

The sixth: that he ruled in favour of one of the two litigants before hearing from the other.

Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the saying of those who claim that he ruled in favour of one of the two litigants before hearing from the other, this is not permissible for the prophets, and likewise the exposing of her husband to being killed. As for those who said that he looked at her until he was satisfied, this is in my view not permissible in any way, because the greedy gaze does not befit the saints who devote themselves to worship, so how much less the prophets, who are the intermediaries of Allah, those granted knowledge of the unseen!

Al-Suddi related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "If I heard a man mention that David (peace be upon him) committed a forbidden act with that woman, I would flog him one hundred and sixty lashes, because the punishment for slandering people is eighty and the punishment for slandering the prophets is one hundred and sixty." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi as well.

Al-Tha'labi said: al-Harith al-A'war reported from 'Ali: "Whoever narrates the story of David as the storytellers relate it, believing it, I would flog him two hundred lashes, for the gravity of what he has committed in accusing the one whom Allah has elevated, whom He chose from His creation as a mercy to the worlds and a proof for the mujtahids."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is among what has not been authentically reported from 'Ali.

If it is said: "What is its ruling according to you?" We say: As for the one who claims that a prophet committed adultery, he is to be executed. As for the one who attributes to him something less than that, such as a glance or touching, people's transmissions differ on this. If someone insists on it and attributes it to him, I would kill him, for that contradicts the discipline that is commanded. As for their saying that his gaze fell upon a woman bathing naked, and when she saw him she let down her hair and covered her body, there is no blame upon him for this by the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah, because the first glance uncovers what is looked at, and the one who looks is not sinful for it. But the second glance has no basis. As for their saying that he intended, if her husband died, to marry her, there is nothing wrong in that, since he did not expose him to death. As for their saying that he proposed upon the proposal of Uriyya, this is false, and the Qur'an and all the exegetical reports refute it.

Ashhab related from Malik who said: It reached me that the dove came and landed near David (peace be upon him), and it was made of gold. When he saw it he was pleased, so he stood to take it, but it was near his hand. He did this twice more, then it flew away, and he followed it with his gaze, and his eye fell upon that woman while she was bathing with long hair. It reached me that he remained prostrate for forty nights until grass grew from the tears of his eyes.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the saying of the exegetes that the bird passed by him, so he intended to take it and followed it, this does not contradict worship, because it is a permissible act, especially since it is lawful, and seeking what is lawful is an obligation. He only followed the bird for its own sake, not for its beauty, for there is no benefit for him in that. Mentioning the beauty of the bird is a foolishness in ignorance. As for the report that it was a golden locust that he followed in order to take it, it was from Allah's bounty, Glorified and Exalted is He, as is reported in the Sahih: "Ayyub (peace be upon him) was bathing naked, when a swarm of golden locusts fell upon him, and he began to gather them up and put them in his garment. Allah, Exalted, said to him: 'O Ayyub, did I not make you wealthy?' He said: 'Yes, my Lord, but there is no wealth for me apart from Your blessing.'"

Al-Qushayri said: David intended to take it to give to a young son of his, but it flew and landed on the window of the house. This was also said by al-Tha'labi, and it has been mentioned before.

The nineteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾, that is, he fell down prostrating. Prostration is sometimes expressed by the term "bowing" (rukū'). The poet said:

"He fell upon his face bowing, and repented to Allah from every sin."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that what is meant by "bowing" here is prostration, for prostration is inclining, and bowing is bending, and each of them enters into the other, but each may be specific to a particular posture. Then this usage came by naming one of them with the other, so prostration was called bowing. Al-Mahdawi said: "Their bowing was prostration." It was also said: "Rather, their prostration was bowing." Muqatil said: "He fell from his bowing into prostration before Allah, Mighty and Majestic," meaning that when he sensed the matter, he stood for prayer, then fell from bowing to prostration, since both involve inclining. "And turned in repentance" means he repented from his wrongdoing and returned to Allah.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Abdullah ibn Tahir, who was a wali (governor) of Ali, asked me about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And he fell down bowing (kharra raki'an)." Is it said of one who is bowing that he "fell down"? I said: No. He said: Then what is the meaning of the verse? I said: Its meaning is: he fell down (prostrating) after having been bowing, that is, he prostrated.

The twentieth matter: Scholars differed over the prostration of Dawud (David), whether it is one of the prostrations of obligation (azaim al-sujud) commanded in the Qur'an or not. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Prophet ﷺ recited on the minbar: "Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder," and when he reached the prostration he descended and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. Then on another day he recited it, and the people tensed (tashazzana) for prostration [[al-tashazzun means preparing oneself and getting ready for something.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is a repentance of a prophet, but I saw you tensing for prostration," and he descended and prostrated. This is the wording of Abu Dawud. In al-Bukhari and others, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: "Sad" is not among the prostrations of the Qur'an, but I saw the Prophet ﷺ prostrating in it. It has also been narrated through a chain from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Sad" is a repentance of a prophet, and there is no prostration in it. And from Ibn Abbas that it is "the repentance of a prophet, and your Prophet is among those commanded to be followed." Ibn al-Arabi said: What I hold is that it is not a place of prostration, but the Prophet ﷺ prostrated in it, so we prostrate following him. The meaning of the prostration is that Dawud prostrated humbly before his Lord, acknowledging his sin and repenting of his error. So whoever prostrates in it should prostrate with this intention, perhaps Allah will forgive him by the sanctity of Dawud whom he followed. Whether or not we say that the law of those before us is law for us, this is a matter legislated in every nation for everyone. And Allah knows best.

The twenty-first matter: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: His words, "And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance," indicate that the prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr) alone is not permissible, because He mentioned bowing with it. What is permissible is to perform two rak'ahs in gratitude; but a single prostration is not. This is because glad tidings used to come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to the imams after him, and it is not transmitted from any of them that he prostrated in gratitude. Had that been done by them, it would have been transmitted widely, since the common people had need to know its permissibility and that it is an act of worship.

I say: In Sunan Ibn Majah, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, the Prophet ﷺ prayed two rak'ahs on the day he was given the news of the head of Abu Jahl. And he narrated from the hadith of Abu Bakrah that the Prophet ﷺ, whenever something pleasing came to him, or something that made him glad, fell down prostrating in gratitude to Allah. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and others.

The twenty-second matter: al-Tirmidhi and others narrated, and the wording is of the latter: A man from the Ansar in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray at night, concealed by a tree, and he was reciting "Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder." When he reached the prostration he prostrated, and the tree prostrated with him. He heard it saying: "O Allah, magnify for me by this prostration a reward, and grant me through it gratitude." I say: Ibn Majah recorded in his Sunan on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: I was with the Prophet ﷺ when a man came to him and said: "Last night, in what the sleeper sees, I seemed to be praying at the base of a tree. I recited the prostration and prostrated, and the tree prostrated with my prostration. I heard it saying: 'O Allah, remove through it from me a burden, write for me through it a reward, and make it for me a store with You.'" Ibn Abbas said: Then I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite "the prostration" and prostrate, and I heard him say in his prostration the like of what the man reported about the words of the tree. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, I saw myself in a dream as if I were under a tree, and the tree was reciting 'Sad'; when it reached the prostration it prostrated in it, and I heard it saying in its prostration: 'O Allah, write for me through it a reward, remove from me through it a burden, grant me through it gratitude, and accept it from me as You accepted the prostration of Your servant Dawud.'" The Prophet ﷺ said to me: "Did you prostrate, O Abu Sa'id?" I said: "No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "You were more worthy of prostration than the tree." Then the Prophet ﷺ recited "Sad" until he reached the prostration and prostrated, then said the like of what the tree had said.

The twenty-third matter: His saying, Exalted is He: "So We forgave him that" (faghafarna lahu dhalik), meaning: So We forgave him his sin. Ibn al-Anbari said: "So We forgave him that" is a complete pause, then you begin: "And indeed for him..." (wa inna lahu). Al-Qushayri said: It is also permissible to pause at "So We forgave him," then begin with "that, and indeed for him" (dhalika wa inna lahu), like His saying: "This! And indeed for the transgressors..." [Sad: 55], meaning: the matter is that.

Ata al-Khurasani and others said: Dawud prostrated for forty days until the pasture grew from the heat of his inner self and his head was submerged. Then he was called: "Is the hungry one to be fed, and the naked one to be clothed?" He wept a weeping which stirred the pasture from the heat of his belly, and he was forgiven and covered by it. He said: "O Lord, this is my sin between me and You, You have forgiven it. But what of so-and-so and so-and-so, men of the Children of Israel, whose children I left orphans and whose wives I left widows?" He said: "O Dawud, on the Day of Resurrection no wrong will pass beyond Me: I will enable him to take from you, then I will ask him to grant you release in exchange for the reward of Paradise." He said: "O Lord, is this how forgiveness is easy?" Then it was said: "O Dawud, raise your head." He went to raise his head, but it had become stuck in the earth, so Jibril came to him and pulled it up from the surface of the earth as sap is pulled from a tree. Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated it from Ibn Jabir from Ata. Al-Walid said: Munir ibn al-Zubayr informed me, saying: So the places of his prostrations adhered to the earth from the skin of his face for as long as Allah willed. Al-Walid said: Ibn Lahi'ah said: He used to say in his prostration: "Glory be to You. This is my drink, my tears, and this is my food, in ashes before me." In another report: He prostrated for forty days, not raising his head except for the obligatory prayer, and he wept until grass grew from his tears. It is also transmitted in a marfu' report from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ: "Dawud remained prostrate for forty nights until grass grew from his tears on his head, and the earth consumed from his forehead, and he was saying in his prostration: 'O Lord, Dawud has slipped a slip, by which the distance between East and West is spread. My Lord, if You do not have mercy on the weakness of Dawud and forgive his sin, You will have made his sin a story among creation after him.' Then Jibril said to him after forty years: 'O Dawud, indeed Allah has forgiven you the concern with which you were concerned.'" Wahb said: Dawud, peace be upon him, was called: "Indeed I have forgiven you." But he did not raise his head until Jibril came to him and said: "Why do you not raise your head, when your Lord has forgiven you?" He said: "O Lord, how, when You do not wrong anyone?" Allah said to Jibril: "Go to Dawud and tell him to go to the grave of Uriyya and seek his pardon from him, for I will make him hear his call." So Dawud put on a woollen garment, sat by the grave of Uriyya and called: "O Uriyya!" He said: "At your service! Who is this who has cut off my pleasure and woken me?" He said: "I am your brother Dawud, asking you to make me blameless, for I exposed you to death." He said: "You exposed me to Paradise, so you are blameless." Al-Hasan and others said: After the sin, Dawud, peace be upon him, would sit only with sinners, saying: "Come to Dawud the sinner." He would not drink any drink without mixing it with the tears of his eyes. He would put dry barley bread in a bowl and weep until it was moistened with his tears, and he would sprinkle ashes and salt on it and eat, saying: "This is the food of sinners." Before the sin he used to stand in prayer half the night and fast half the time. After the sin he fasted all the time and stood all night, and he said: "O Lord, place my sin in my palm." So his sin became inscribed in his palm. He would not spread it out for food or drink or anything without seeing it, and it made him weep. Even if a cup was brought to him, two-thirds water, when he took it he saw his sin, and he would not set it down from his lips until his tears overflowed. Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated: Abu Amr al-Awza'i told me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The likeness of the eyes of Dawud is like two water-skins dripping, and the tears had furrowed the face of Dawud like water furrowing the earth." Al-Walid said: Uthman ibn al-Atika told us that he was in the words of Dawud, since he was free of sin, the intensity of his saying about the sinners, if he was saying: "O Allah, do not forgive the sinners." Then he came to say: "O Allah, Lord, forgive the sinners so that You may forgive Dawud along with them. Glory be to the Creator of light. My God, I went out asking the physicians of Your servants to cure my sin, but all of them point me to You. My God, I committed a sin of which I fear You will make its harvest Your punishment on the Day of Resurrection if You do not forgive it. Glory be to the Creator of light. My God, when I remember my sin the earth is straitened upon me despite its vastness, and when I remember Your mercy my soul returns to me." In a report: When Dawud, peace be upon him, climbed the minbar, he raised his right hand and faced the people with it to show them the engraving of his sin. He would call out: "My God! When I remember my sin the earth is straitened upon me despite its vastness, and when I remember Your mercy my soul returns to me. Lord! Forgive the sinners so that You may forgive Dawud along with them." He used to sit on seven mats of palm fiber stuffed with ashes, and his tears would collect beneath his feet until they passed through all the mats. When it was the day of his lamentation, his herald would call out in the roads, markets, valleys, ravines, on the tops of mountains and at the mouths of caves: "Behold, this is the day of Dawud's lamentation. Whoever wishes to weep over his sin, let him come to Dawud and join him in it." Then the wanderers would descend from the caves and valleys.

...the voices resound around his pulpit, while the wild beasts, the predators and the birds are gathered (in devotion), and the Children of Israel are around his pulpit. When he begins the lamentation and wailing, and the burning sorrow stirs the springs of his tears, the congregation becomes one single outcry of mourning and weeping, until a great number of people die around his pulpit on that same day.

It is said that Dawud (peace be upon him) died suddenly on a Saturday. The Angel of Death came to him while he was ascending and descending his mihrab (prayer niche), and said: "I have come to take your soul." He said: "Leave me until I descend or ascend." The Angel said: "There is no way for that. The days, the months, the years, the traces and the provisions have come to an end, and after them you will leave no trace." He said: So Dawud prostrated upon a step of the stairway, and his soul was taken in that state.

Between him and Musa (peace be upon them both) were five hundred and ninety-nine years. It is also said: seventy-nine. He lived one hundred years, and he bequeathed the caliphate to his son Sulayman.

The twenty-fourth (issue): His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a station of nearness and a good return﴾.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muhammad ibn Qays said: "And indeed, for him with Us is a station of nearness" means nearness (qurbah) after forgiveness. "And a good return" — they both said: "By Allah, the first to drink from the cup on the Day of Resurrection will be Dawud."

Mujahid said, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Umar: "Al-Zulfa" is drawing near to Allah, mighty and majestic, on the Day of Resurrection.

And on the authority of Mujahid: Dawud will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with his sin inscribed in his hand. When he sees the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, he will find no refuge from them except to take shelter in the mercy of Allah, the Exalted. He said: Then he will see his sin and become distressed, and it will be said to him, "Here!" Then he will see it again and become distressed, and it will be said to him, "Here!" Then he will see it again and become distressed, and it will be said to him, "Here!" [[This addition is required by the context, and is indicated by what occurs at the end of the story.]] "Until he draws near and is calmed." That is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a station of nearness and a good return﴾.

al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it. He said: Al-Fadl ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Malik ibn al-Asbagh narrated to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Fazari narrated to us, on the authority of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, on the authority of Mujahid, and he mentioned it.

al-Tirmidhi said: I used to pass over these verses for a long time without the meaning of His saying, "Our Lord, hasten for us our qitt," becoming clear to me. The qitt (the written record, a scroll) in the language is the sheet (sahifah). That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19], and said to them: "You will find all of this in your records, which will be given to you in your left hands." They said: "Our Lord, hasten for us our qitt," meaning our record, "before the Day of Reckoning." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the one of strength﴾, and He related the story of his sin to its end. I used to say: He commanded him to be patient over what they say, and commanded him to remember Dawud. What was intended by this remembrance, and how was this connected to that? I could not settle on anything that would calm my heart, until Allah guided me to it one day, and it was inspired in me that these people denied that they would be given their records in their left hands, containing their sins and errors, mocking the command of Allah, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our qitt before the Day of Reckoning﴾. This pained him because of their mockery. So He commanded him to be patient over their words, and to remember His servant Dawud, who asked for his sin to be hastened so that he would see it inscribed in his palm. So there befell him what befell him, namely that whenever he saw it he trembled, and the cup was filled with his tears, and whenever he saw it he wept until his tears soaked through seven mats of palm fiber stuffed with ashes. [[Perhaps the original reads: "until his tears soaked through..." etc.]] He only asked for it after forgiveness and after the guarantee against the claim of the adversary, and after Allah, blessed and exalted is His name, had granted him that (sin) as a gift, and he is His beloved, His friend and His chosen one. So seeing the inscription of the sin in its own form, with this rank, affected him in this way. How then would the enemies of Allah, His disobedient creatures and the people of His disgrace be treated, if their records were hastened for them, and they looked upon the forms of those sins which they committed in disbelief and denial, and what would befall them when they look at them in those records? Allah has informed us about them, saying: ﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say: "Woe to us! What is this record? It leaves nothing small or great but it has counted it."﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. So Dawud, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, with forgiveness, glad tidings and kindness, could not endure the sight of the form of it.

And we have related in a hadith: When he sees it inscribed in his palm on the Day of Resurrection, he becomes distressed until it is said to him, "Here!" Then he sees it and becomes distressed, then it is said, "Here!" Then he sees it and becomes distressed, until he draws near and is calmed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 26:

There are five issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have made you a khalifah (successor, vicegerent) upon the earth﴾, meaning: We have given you dominion so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and so you succeed those who were before you among the prophets and the righteous imams. The discussion of the khalifah (caliph) and its rulings has already passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 263 and following, second or third edition.]], and it has been fully treated, praise be to God.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, meaning: with justice. This is a command of obligation. This is connected to what precedes it, for what Dawud was rebuked for was his asking for the woman from her husband, and that is not justice. So after this it was said to him: "So judge between the people with justice, and do not follow desire," meaning: do not be guided by your own desire that opposes the command of God, "for it will lead you astray from the path of God," meaning: from the way of Paradise. "Indeed, those who stray from the path of God," meaning: they deviate from it and abandon it, "will have a severe punishment" in the Fire "for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning," meaning: for having abandoned walking the path of God. So His saying "forgotten" means they abandoned faith in it, or abandoned acting upon it, and so they became like those who forget. Then it has been said: this was addressed to Dawud after God had honored him with prophethood. And it has been said: after He had accepted his repentance and forgiven his error.

The third: The basis in matters of judgment is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾, and His saying: ﴿And that you judge between them by what God has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may judge between the people by what God has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa': 105], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for God, witnesses in justice﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], to the end of the verse. The discussion of this has already passed [[See vol. 5, p. 375 and following, and vol. 6, p. 109 and following, and p. 212, second edition.]].

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying, exalted is He: "O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth, so judge between the people with truth and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the path of God." He said: If two litigants come before you and you have a inclination toward one of them, then do not desire in yourself that the truth be for him so that he prevails over his companion [[yufliju 'ala sahibihi: to prevail over and triumph over him.]]. For if you do so, I will erase your name from My prophethood, and then you will not be My khalifah nor among the people of My honor. This indicates the obligation of judging by truth, and that one should not incline toward either of the two disputants because of kinship, or hope of benefit, or any cause that calls for inclination, such as companionship or friendship, or other things.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon him, was only tested because two litigants came before him, and he desired that the truth be for one of them.

'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad said: It reached me that a judge in the time of the Children of Israel, so great was his diligence, asked his Lord to make for him a sign between himself and Him: whenever he judged by truth he would know it, and whenever he fell short he would know it. It was said to him: Enter your house, then stretch your hand against your wall, then look to where your fingers reach on the wall, and draw a line there. When you rise from the seat of judgment, return to that line and stretch your hand toward it, for whenever you are upon the truth you will reach it, and if you fall short of the truth, it will fall short of you. So he would go out to judgment with diligence, and he would not judge except by truth. When he rose from his seat and was free, he would not taste food or drink, nor would he approach his family with anything of matters until he came to that line. When he reached it, he praised God, and then he would go to all that God had made lawful for him of family, food, or drink. One day, while he was in the seat of judgment, two men came to him seeking him, and it occurred to him that they wanted to dispute before him, and one of them was his friend and companion. His heart was stirred toward him out of love that the truth would be for him, so that he would decide in his favor. When they spoke, the truth turned against his friend, and he ruled against him. When he rose from his seat, he went to his line as he would go every day, and he stretched his hand toward the line, and behold, the line had gone and had risen up to the ceiling, and he could not reach it. He fell down prostrate, saying: "O my Lord, a thing I did not intend and did not want, so make it clear to me." It was said to him: Do you think that God, exalted is He, did not perceive the treachery of your heart, when you loved that the truth would be for your friend so that you would judge for him by it? You desired it and loved it, but God has returned the truth to its people while you were unwilling.

And from Layth, who said: Two litigants came before 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he had them stand, then they came back and he had them stand, then they came back and he decided between them. He was asked about that, and he said: "The two of them came before me, and I found in one of them something I did not find in his companion, and I disliked to decide between them on that basis. Then they came back and I found some of that in him, then they came back and that had gone, so I decided between them."

And al-Sha'bi said: There was a dispute between 'Umar and Ubayy, and they went to Zayd ibn Thabit for judgment. When they entered upon him, he gestured to 'Umar toward his cushion, and 'Umar said: "This is the first of your injustice. Seat me and him in one seat." So they both sat before him.

The fifth: This verse prohibits a judge from ruling on his own knowledge, for if judges were empowered to rule by their own knowledge, none of them would refrain, whenever he wished to protect his ally and destroy his enemy, from claiming knowledge of what he ruled upon. Similar to this has been related from a group of the Companions, among them Abu Bakr, who said: "If I saw a man committing one of God's hadd punishments, I would not take him until another than me testifies to it." It is also related that a woman came to 'Umar and said to him: "Judge for me against so-and-so for such-and-such, for you know what I have from him." He said to her: "If you want me to bear witness for you, then yes; but as for judgment, no." In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) decided by an oath and a witness. And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he bought a horse, and the seller denied it, and he did not rule against him by his own knowledge, but said: "Who will bear witness for me?" Khuzaymah stood up and testified, and he ruled. Abu Dawud and others recorded the hadith. And it has passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. 405, first or second edition.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 27–29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ — that is, in jest and play. That is, We created them only for a true purpose, which is the indication of Our power. "That is the assumption of those who disbelieve" — that is, the reckoning of those who disbelieve that Allah created them in vain. "So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire." Then He mentioned their opposite, and said: "Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds as the corrupters on the earth?" The mim here is a connecting particle (silah); its estimated form is: "Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds [like] the corrupters on the earth?" In this there is a refutation of the Murji'ah (Murji'ah, a sect who deferred judgment on the matter of faith and works), for they say: it is permissible that the corrupter be equal to the righteous, or have a higher rank than him. And after it also: "Or shall We make the pious like the wicked?" That is, shall We make the companions of Muhammad, peace be upon him, like the disbelievers? This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said that it is general concerning the pious Muslims and the wicked disbelievers, and this is the better view, and it is a refutation of those who deny the Resurrection, who made the destination of the obedient and the disobedient one and the same.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A Book﴾ — that is, this is a Book "which We have sent down to you, blessed," O Muhammad, "that they may ponder over its verses" — that is, that they may contemplate (li-yatadabbaru), so the taa' was assimilated into the daal. In this is evidence of the obligation of knowing the meanings of the Qur'an, and evidence that tartil (measured, deliberate recitation) is better than hadhdh (hasty recitation) [[Al-hadhdh: speed of recitation.]], since contemplation is not valid with hasty recitation, as we have explained in the book al-Tadhkar. Al-Hasan said: "Contemplating the verses of Allah is following them." The reading of the common people is "liyaddabbaru." Abu Hanifah and Shaybah read "litadabbaru" with a taa' and a lightened daal, and this is the reading of 'Ali [[Al-Alusi mentions that 'Ali read "liyatadabbaru" with a taa' after the yaa', and likewise in al-Bahr by Abu Hayyan.]], may Allah be pleased with him. The original is "litatadabbaru," and one of the two taa's was deleted for lightness. "And that those of understanding may take heed" — that is, the people of intellect; its singular is lubb, and it has been pluralized as alub, just as bu's is pluralized as abu's, and nu'm as an'um. Abu Talib said:

"My heart is inclined toward him, its lubbs raised high."

And at times they show the doubling in the necessity of poetry. Al-Kumayt said:

"To you, O family of the Prophet, I have turned my gaze, and my heart's yearnings are thirsty and longing (alabb)."
