**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 44:**

In this verse there are seven issues.

**The first issue:** Ayyub (Job) had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes. There are four opinions about the cause of this.

The first is what Ibn 'Abbas related: Iblis met her in the form of a physician and she asked him to treat Ayyub. He said, "I will treat him on condition that when he is cured he says, 'You have cured me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said, "Yes." So she advised Ayyub accordingly, and he swore that he would strike her. He said, "Woe to you! That was Satan."

The second is what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib related: she brought him more bread than she usually brought, so he feared she had stolen it, and he swore that he would strike her.

The third is what Yahya ibn Sallam and others related: Satan incited her to persuade Ayyub to slaughter a young goat as an offering to him, and that he would be healed. She mentioned this to him, so he swore that he would strike her one hundred times if he recovered.

The fourth: it is said that she sold her locks of hair for two loaves of bread, since she found nothing to bring to Ayyub. Ayyub used to lean on her when he wanted to stand up, so for this reason he swore that he would strike her. When God healed him, He commanded him to take a bundle (*dighth*) and strike with it. So he took about one hundred palm-spathes (*shamarikh*) and struck her with them in a single blow. It is said that the *dighth* is a handful of grass mixed with green and dry parts. Ibn 'Abbas said it is a cluster of palm dates together with its stalks.

**The second issue:** This verse includes the permissibility of a man striking his wife for discipline (*ta'dib*). Ayyub's wife had done wrong, so he swore to strike her one hundred times, and God commanded him to strike her with a cluster of palm dates. This is not permitted in the prescribed punishments (*hudud*). God commanded him to do this only so that he would not strike his wife beyond the limit of discipline. A husband is not permitted to strike his wife beyond the limit of discipline, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Strike them, but not severely" (*wa-idribuhunna darban ghayra mubarrih*), as explained previously in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 172 onward, first or second edition.]].

**The third issue:** The scholars differed over whether this ruling is general or specific to Ayyub alone. It is related from Mujahid that it is general for people; Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned this. It is related from al-Qushayri that it is specific to Ayyub. Al-Mahdawi related from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that he held the ruling to remain in force: if one strikes with one hundred rods or the like in a single blow, one fulfils the oath (*barra*). Al-Shafi'i related something similar. Something similar is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the seat on which a slave-girl had conceived, when he ordered that she be struck with a cluster containing one hundred shoots in a single blow.

Al-Qushayri said: It was asked of 'Ata', "Is this acted upon today?" He said, "The Quran was revealed only to be acted upon and followed."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is related from 'Ata' that it was specific to Ayyub. Likewise Abu Zayd related from Ibn al-Qasim from Malik: whoever swears that he will strike his slave one hundred times, and gathers them and strikes him with them in a single blow, has not fulfilled his oath. Some of our scholars said: Malik means God's words, ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48], that is, this ruling has been abrogated (*mansukh*) by our law.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been transmitted to us from 'Ali that he struck al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah forty lashes with a whip that had two ends. Malik rejected this and recited God's words, ﴿Strike each of them one hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur 24:2]. This is also the position of the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*).

Al-Shafi'i relied for his view on a hadith, though its chain of transmission has been criticised. God knows best.

I say: The hadith on which al-Shafi'i relied was recorded by Abu Dawud in his *Sunan*. He said: Ahmad ibn Sa'id al-Hamdani narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Yunus informed me from Ibn Shihab, who said: Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf informed me that one of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the Ansar informed him that a man among them fell ill until he was worn away, becoming just skin over bone. A slave-girl belonging to one of them came in to him, and he was aroused by her and had intercourse with her. When the men of his people came in to visit him, he told them about this and said, "Ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a ruling for me, for I have had intercourse with a slave-girl who came in to me." They mentioned this to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said, "We have not seen anyone suffer harm like what he is suffering. If we carried him to you, his bones would fall apart; he is nothing but skin over bone." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered that they take for him one hundred shoots and strike him with them in a single blow.

Al-Shafi'i said: If someone swears that he will strike so-and-so one hundred lashes, or a strike, and he does not say "a severe strike" and does not intend that in his heart, then a strike like the one mentioned in the verse suffices for him and he does not break his oath.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: If a man swears that he will strike his slave one hundred times, and he strikes him gently, he has fulfilled his oath according to al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion. Malik said: A strike is only a strike that causes pain.

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿and do not break your oath﴾ [*wa-la tahnath*], are evidence that an exception (*istithna'*) in an oath does not nullify its ruling when it is delayed. The discussion of this has already passed in *al-Ma'idah* [[See vol. 6, p. 272 onward, first or second edition.]]. One says *hanatha fi yaminihi yahnathu* when he does not fulfil his oath by it. According to the Kufans, the *waw* is redundant (*muqhamah*), meaning: "Strike, do not break [your oath]."

**The fifth issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: God's words, ﴿So strike with it and do not break your oath﴾, indicate one of two possibilities. Either there was no expiation (*kaffarah*) in their law, and there was only fulfilment (*barr*) or breaking (*hinth*) of the oath; or what was uttered by him was a vow (*nadhr*) and not an oath. When the vow is specified, there is no expiation for it according to Malik and Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said: For every vow there is an expiation.

I say: His statement that there was no expiation in their law is not correct, for when Ayyub, upon him be peace, remained in affliction for eighteen years, as in the hadith of Ibn Shihab, his two companions said to him: "You have committed a sin that I do not think anyone has ever committed." Ayyub (ﷺ) said: "I do not know what you are saying, except that my Lord, mighty and majestic, knows that I used to pass by two men who were quarrelling, and each of them swore by God, or by a group of people who were disputing, and I would return to my family and make expiation for their oaths, desiring that no one should sin by mentioning Him, and that no one should mention Him except rightfully [[In one copy: 'except we.']]." Then he called out to his Lord: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:83], and he mentioned the hadith.

So this hadith teaches you that expiation was part of the law of Ayyub, and that whoever makes expiation on behalf of another without his permission has discharged the obligation on his behalf, and the expiation has fallen from him.

**The sixth issue:** Some of the ignorant among the ascetics (*al-mutazahhidah*) and the crude among the Sufis (*al-mutasawwifah*) cited God's words to Ayyub, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [38:42], as evidence for the permissibility of dancing (*raqs*). Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: This is a weak argument, for if he had been commanded to strike the foot in joy, they would have some basis for it; but he was commanded to strike the ground with his foot so that water would spring forth.

Ibn 'Aqil said: Where is the evidence in a person afflicted, who at the lifting of his affliction was commanded to strike the ground with his foot so that water would spring forth, as a miracle, of dancing? And if it is permissible that moving a foot which has been loosened by the crawling of lice is evidence for the permissibility of dancing in Islam, then it is permissible also to take God's words to Musa, ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:60], as evidence for striking the *muhadd* with rods! [[Thus in the original; in some copies it reads "al-makhad" with a *kha'*.]] We seek refuge in God from playing with the Sharia.

Some of their deficient ones (*qasiriyyihim*) have argued that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali: "You are from me and I am from you," and so he [danced]. And Ja'far [danced] when he said: "You resemble me in form and in character" (*ashbahta khalqi wa-khuluqi*). And he said to Zayd: "You are our brother and our client (*mawlana*)," and so he [danced]. Some of them argued that the Abyssinians danced (*zafanat*) while the Prophet (ﷺ) watched them.

The answer: As for the *'ajal* (the jumping of the calf), it is a kind of action performed at joy, so where is it in relation to dancing? Likewise the *zafn* of the Abyssinians is a kind of action performed when meeting for war.

**The seventh issue:** God's words, ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾, meaning patient over the affliction. ﴿An excellent servant; indeed, he was one who constantly turned back (to God)﴾, meaning he was repentant (*tawwab*), returning (*raj-jA'*), obedient (*muti'*).

Sufyan was asked about two servants: one of them was afflicted and was patient, and the other was blessed and was grateful. He said: Both are equal, because God praised two servants, one patient and the other grateful, with one and the same praise. He said, describing Ayyub: ﴿An excellent servant; indeed, he was one who constantly turned back﴾, and he said, describing Sulayman: ﴿An excellent servant; indeed, he was one who constantly turned back﴾.

I say: The author of *al-Qut* has refuted this statement, and he used the story of Ayyub as evidence for the superiority of the poor over the rich, and he mentioned many words to strengthen his argument. We have mentioned this elsewhere in the book *Manhaj al-'Ibad wa-Mahajjat al-Salikin wa-al-Zuhhad*. But he overlooked the fact that Ayyub, upon him be peace, was among the wealthy prophets, both before the affliction and after it; he was only afflicted with the loss of his property and children and the severe disease in his body. Likewise the prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, were patient over what they were tested and tried with. Ayyub, upon him be peace, entered the affliction in a certain state and came out of it as he had entered it; no state or speech of his changed. Thus he and Sulayman [[The pronoun refers to Sulayman, upon him be peace.]] shared the intended meaning, which is the lack of change by which some people surpass others. In this sense, the grateful rich and the patient poor are equal, and this is as Sufyan said. God knows best.

In the hadith of Ibn Shihab from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ayyub went out for his need, as he used to go out. God revealed to him: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink﴾ [38:42]. So he bathed, and God restored his flesh, his hair and his skin to the best they had been. Then he drank, and God removed from his inside every pain and weakness. God sent down to him two white garments from heaven, and he wrapped himself in one and put on the other. Then he began walking toward his home, and he was slow (*ra'a*) in reaching his wife. So she came out until she met him, and she did not recognise him. She greeted him and said, 'May God have mercy on you, have you seen this afflicted man?' He said, 'Who is he?' She said, 'The prophet of God, Ayyub. By God, I have never seen anyone more like him than you, when he was healthy.' He said, 'Indeed, I am Ayyub,' and he took a bundle (*dighth*) and struck her with it." Ibn Shihab claimed that this bundle was *thumam* [[*Al-tamam*: a weak plant that has fronds or resembles fronds.]]. God restored to him his family and as many more with them. Then a cloud came and poured down upon the threshing floor of his wheat with gold until it was full, and another cloud came to the threshing floor of his barley and his pulses [[*Al-qatani*: grains that are stored, such as chickpeas, lentils, beans and the like.]], and it poured silver upon them until it was full.

Also, God's words: ﴿And remember Our servants Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, possessors of strength and insight. Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the abode. And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent﴾ [38:45–47].

**Allah's words: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾.** Ibn 'Abbas recited "'abdana" (our servant) with a sound chain of transmission, narrated by Ibn 'Uyaynah from 'Amr from 'Ata' from him. This is also the reading of Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir. According to this reading, "Ibrahim" is in apposition (badal) to "'abdana," and "Ishaq and Ya'qub" are conjoined ( 'atf). The reading in the plural is clearer, and it is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, and in that case "Ibrahim" and what follows it are in apposition (badal).

Al-Nahhas said: The explanation of this from the Arabic language is that when you say, "I saw our companions Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid," then Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid are in apposition, and they are the companions. When you say, "I saw our companion Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid," then Zayd alone is in apposition, and he is our companion, while Zayd and 'Amr are conjoined to "our companion," and they are not included in the companionship except by evidence other than this. However, it is known that His words, "and Ishaq and Ya'qub," are included in the servitude.

Whoever argued from this verse that the one who was sacrificed was Isaac and not Ishmael used it as evidence, and this is the correct view, as we have mentioned in the book "al-I'lam bi-Mawlid al-Nabi" (ﷺ).

**"Possessors of strength and insight."** Al-Nahhas said: As for "al-absar" (insight), there is agreement on its interpretation as insights into the religion and knowledge. As for "al-aydi" (strength), its interpretation is disputed. The people of tafsir say that it means strength in religion. Others say that "al-aydi" is the plural of "yad," which means blessing, meaning they are people of blessings, that is, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has bestowed favour. It was also said: they are people of blessings and goodness, because they did good and sent forward good deeds. This is the choice of al-Tabari.

**"And indeed they are with Us among the chosen, the excellent."** That is, those whom He chose from impurities and selected for His message. "Mustafayn" is the plural of "mustafa," and the original form is "mustafta," which has already been discussed in al-Baqarah at His words, "Indeed, Allah has chosen for you the religion" (2:132). [[See vol. 2, p. 133, in the commentary on His words "And We had certainly chosen him in this world" (2:130), where the derivation of the word is discussed; it is not in the verse mentioned.]] "Al-akhyar" is the plural of "khayyir."

Al-A'mash, 'Abd al-Warith, al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "uli al-aydi" without a ya' both in continuation and in pause, meaning "possessors of strength in obedience to Allah." It is also permissible that it has the same meaning as the reading of the majority, with the ya' omitted for lightness.

**Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾.** The common reading is "bi-khalisatin" with tanwin, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Nafi', Shayba, Abu Ja'far and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read "bi-khalisati dhikra al-dar" with the idafa (construct). Whoever puts tanwin on "khalisatin," then "dhikra al-dar" is in apposition to it. The sense is: We purified them by their remembering the Hereafter, preparing for it, desiring it, and causing people to desire it. It is also permissible that "khalisatin" is a verbal noun (masdar) of "khalasa," and "dhikra" is in the nominative position as its agent, and the meaning is: We purified them in that the remembrance of the Abode became pure for them, that is, the reminder of the Hereafter. It is also permissible that "khalisatin" is a verbal noun of "akhlasa," and the tanwin is dropped, so "dhikra" in this case is in the accusative position, the sense being: by their sincerely making the remembrance of the Abode. "The Abode" may refer to this world, meaning that they remember this world and renounce it, and that a good commendation of them remains for them, as He said: ﴿And We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, exalted﴾ [Maryam: 50]. It may also refer to the Hereafter and the reminding of creation of it. Whoever puts the idafa to "khalisatin" to "al-dar," then it is a verbal noun meaning sincerity, and "dhikra" is the object, to which the verbal noun is added, meaning: by their sincerity in the remembrance of the Abode. It is also permissible that the verbal noun is added to the agent, and "khalisa" is a verbal noun meaning purity, that is, by the purity of the remembrance of the Abode for them, and "the Abode" is the Hereafter or this world, as previously explained.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "akhlasahum" is by the mention of the Hereafter, that is, they remember the Hereafter, desire it, and renounce this world. Mujahid said: The meaning is, "We purified them by making Paradise mentioned to them."

﴿And remember Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl; each of them is among the best.﴾ The mention of al-Yasa' has already passed in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 33, first or second edition.]], and the mention of Dhul-Kifl in "al-Anbiya'" [[See vol. 11, p. 327, first or second edition.]]. "Each of them is among the best" means each of them is among those chosen for prophethood. "This is a reminder" means this is a fine reputation in this world and an honour by which they will be remembered in this world forever. "And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return" means that, along with this fine remembrance in this world, they have an excellent final destination in the Hereafter. Then He explained this by saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden⦆ ("Eden" in the language means settling, as one says: "'adana bil-makan" when one settles in a place). 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: "Indeed, in Paradise there is a palace called 'Adn, around which are the towers and the meadows. In it are five thousand doors, and at each door are five thousand ḥibar [[al-ḥibara, with a kasra or fatha on the ḥa', is a type of striped Yemeni cloth.]]. No one enters it except a prophet, a truthful one (ṣiddīq), or a martyr." ﴿with doors open for them⦆: "mufattaḥatan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and "al-abwāb" is in the nominative because it is the substitute for the unnamed agent. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning the doors of it are opened for them. Al-Farra' said: its doors are opened for them. Al-Farra' also permitted "mufattaḥatan lahumu al-abwābu" with the accusative. Al-Farra' said: meaning "mufattaḥatu al-abwāb" [open of doors], then you added tanwīn, so it became accusative. He and Sibawayh recited:

"And we take after him the tail of a life... whose back is bent, having no hump."

[[The poem is by al-Nabigha, and the evidence in it is that "al-zahr" (back) is accusative by "ajabb" on the intention of tanwīn. He described the illness of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, and that if he died people would be in the worst state and the narrowest living, and would cling to him like the tail of a camel "ajabb," which is one with no hump due to emaciation.]]

He said "mufattaḥatan" and not "maftūḥatan" because they are opened for them by command, not by touch. Al-Ḥasan said: it speaks, "Open," and it opens; "Close," and it closes. It was also said: the angels open the doors for them.

﴿Reclining therein⦆ is a ḥāl placed before its governing verb, which is His saying "yad'ūna fīhā" (they call for therein). That is, they call for fruits and drinks in the gardens while reclining in them. ﴿With abundant fruit⦆ means with various kinds of fruits, ﴿and drink⦆ means and abundant drink; the adjective was omitted because the context indicates it.

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances⦆ means they restrain their gaze upon their husbands and do not look at anyone else. This has already passed in "al-Saffat" [[See p. 80 of this part.]]. ﴿Equal in age⦆ means of the same age, born at the same time, and equal in beauty and youth, all of them thirty-three years old. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the human women. "Atrāb" is the plural of "tirb," and it is an adjective for "qāṣirāt," because "qāṣirāt" is indefinite even though it is attached to a definite noun. The evidence for this is that "al-" and "lām" enter upon it, as in the saying:

"Of those restraining their glances, if a small child crawled... and of the mites above her robe, it would have left a mark."

[[The poet is Imru' al-Qays. "Maḥwal" means small. "Al-itb" is a woman's garment. Its sleeve is split so it is worn without a sleeve or a collar.]]

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning⦆ means this is the reward you were promised. The reading of the majority is with the "tā'" (you), meaning "what you are promised, O believers." Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muḥaysin, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the "yā'" (third person), as a report, and this is the reading of al-Sulami and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, due to His saying "And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return," which is a report. ﴿For the Day of Reckoning⦆ means on the Day of Reckoning. Al-A'sha said:

"The humiliators, what for them... in a time of evil, until it awakens, then they awake."

"Of those restraining their glances, if a small child crawled... and of the mites above her robe, it would have left a mark."

[[The poet is Imru' al-Qays. "Maḥwal" means small. "Al-itb" is a woman's garment. Its sleeve is split so it is worn without a sleeve or a collar.]]

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning⦆ means this is the reward you were promised. The reading of the majority is with the "tā'" (you), meaning "what you are promised, O believers." Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muḥaysin, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the "yā'" (third person), as a report, and this is the reading of al-Sulami and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, due to His saying "And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return," which is a report. ﴿For the Day of Reckoning⦆ means on the Day of Reckoning. Al-A'sha said:

"The humiliators, what for them... in a time of evil, until it awakens, then they awake."

That is, in a time of evil.

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no end⦆ is evidence that the bounty of Paradise is everlasting and does not cease, as He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted⦆ [Hud: 108], and He said: "For them is a reward uninterrupted" [al-Tin: 6].

﴿This is so; and indeed, for the rebellious is an evil place of return﴾. When He mentioned what is for the God-fearing, He mentioned what is for the rebellious. Then one begins with "and indeed for the rebellious," who are those who denied the messengers.

Then He explained this with His words: ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting-place﴾, meaning, wretched is what they prepared for themselves, or wretched is the bed for them. From this comes the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabi). It was also said that there is an omission here, meaning, "wretched is the place of the resting-place." It was also said: meaning, this is what I have described for these God-fearing people. Then He said: ﴿And indeed for the rebellious is an evil place of return﴾, so one also pauses at "this."

His words: ﴿This; so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, icy liquid﴾. "This" is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is "boiling water," in inverted order, meaning: this is boiling water and dark liquid, so let them taste it. One does not pause at "so let them taste it." It is also permissible for "this" to be in the nominative position as the subject, and "so let them taste it" to be in the position of the predicate, with the "fa'" (fa) entering for the sake of the alerting force in "this." One then pauses at "so let them taste it," and "boiling water" is nominative by the assumption of "this is boiling water."

Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible that the meaning is "the matter is this," and "boiling water and dark liquid," if you do not make them the predicate, are nominative with the meaning "it is boiling water and dark liquid." Al-Farra' makes them nominative with the meaning "from it is boiling water, and from it is dark liquid," and he recited:

*"Until, when the dawn lit up in the dimness, and the herbage was left, some twisted and some mown."*

Another said [its speaker is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, describing a she-camel by which one draws water. "Qatab" is the saddle-frame of the water-wheel; "gharb" is a large bucket. "Insahaqa" means it passed and wore away after its flow]:

*"She has goods and helpers who walk with her, a saddle-frame and a great bucket which, when emptied, wore away."*

It is also permissible that "this" is in the accusative position by an implied verb which "so let them taste it" explains, as you say: "Zayd, strike him." The accusative in this case is preferable. One pauses at "so let them taste it," and one begins with "boiling water and dark liquid," with the assumption of "the matter is boiling water and dark liquid."

The reading of the people of Medina, the people of Basra, and some of the Kufans is with the lightening of the sin in "wa-ghassaq" (and dark liquid). Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-ghassaq" with emphasis (tashdid). According to al-Akhfash, they are two dialects with one meaning. It was also said that their meanings differ. Whoever lightens it treats it as a noun, like "adhab" (torment), "jawab" (answer), and "sawab" (correctness). Whoever emphasizes it says it is an active participle (ism fa'il) shifted to the form "fa''al" for intensification, like "darrab" (one who strikes much) and "qattal" (one who kills much). It is of the form "fa''al" from "ghasaqa, yaghsiqu," so one says "ghassaq" and "ghasiq."

Ibn Abbas said: it is the zamhareer (extreme cold), which frightens them with its cold. Mujahid and Muqatil said: it is the cold snow whose cold has reached its limit. Others said: it burns with its cold just as boiling water burns with its heat. Abdullah ibn Amr said: it is thick pus; if one drop of it fell in the east, it would make those in the west stink, and if one drop of it fell in the west, it would make those in the east stink. Qatadah said: it is what flows from the private parts of fornicators, and from the stench of the flesh and skins of the disbelievers, from pus, matter, and stench. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is the essence (usara) of the people of the Fire. This view is closer to the language. It is said: "ghasaqa al-jurh, yaghsiqu, ghasqan" when a yellow water came out of it. The poet said:

*"When I remember life and its sweetness, tears from the eye flow down toward me, dark."*

Meaning, cold. It is said: "laylun ghasiq" (a dark night), because it is colder than the day. Al-Suddi said: "al-ghassaq" is what flows from their eyes and their tears, which they are given to drink along with the boiling water. Ibn Zayd said: "al-hamim" is the tears of their eyes, which are gathered in the pools of the Fire and they are given to drink, and "al-sadid" is what comes out of their skins. The preferred reading on this view is "wa-ghassaq," so that it is like "sayyal" (flowing). Ka'b said: "al-ghassaq" is a spring in Hell into which the poison of every venomous creature, such as scorpions and snakes, flows. It was also said: it is derived from darkness and blackness. "Al-ghasaq" is the first darkness of the night, and "ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu" means the night became dark.

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "If a bucket of ghassaq were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink." I say: this is closer to the first derivation, as we have explained, except that it is possible that "al-ghassaq," with its flowing, is black and dark, so both derivations are valid. And God knows best.

His words: ﴿And other punishments of its kind, in pairs﴾. Abu Amr read "wa-ukhar," the plural of "ukhra," like "al-kubra" and "al-kubar." The rest read "wa-akhar," singular masculine. Abu Amr objected to "wa-akhar" because of His words "in pairs" (azwaj), meaning that one does not give news of one thing about a group. Asim al-Jahdari objected to "wa-ukhar," and said: if it were "wa-ukhar," it would be "min shaklihi" (of its kind). Both objections do not hold, and both readings are sound. "Wa-akhar" means "and another punishment besides the boiling water and the dark liquid." "Min shaklihi" (of its kind): Qatadah said: "of its likeness." Ibn Mas'ud said: it is the zamhareer.

"Wa-akhar" is in the nominative position as the subject, "azwaj" is a second subject, "min shaklihi" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "akhar." It is also permissible that "wa-akhar" is the subject and the predicate is implied, indicated by "this; so let them taste it: boiling water and dark liquid," because in it is evidence that it is for them. It is as if he said: "and for them is another," and "min shaklihi azwaj" is an attribute of "akhar," so the subject is specified by the attribute, and "azwaj" is nominative by the adverbial phrase. Whoever reads "wa-ukhar" means "and kinds of punishment, others." Whoever reads it in the plural while meaning the zamhareer does so because he made the zamhareer into kinds, so he used the plural because the kinds differ. Or because he made for each part of it a zamhareer, then pluralized it, as they say: "shabat mafariquh" (his temples turned grey). Or because it is a plural in view of what the speech indicates of the permissibility of plurality, since he placed the zamhareer, which is the extreme of cold, opposite the plural in His words: "this; so let them taste it: boiling water and dark liquid."

The pronoun in "shaklihi" may refer to the boiling water or to the dark liquid. Or it may refer to the meaning of "wa-akhar min shaklihi" as we mentioned. In the plural reading, "ukhar" is nominative as the subject, "min shaklihi" is an attribute of it, and there is a reference in it returning to the subject, and "azwaj" is the predicate of the subject. It is not permissible to take it as the assumption "and for them are others," with "min shaklihi" as an attribute of "ukhar," and "azwaj" being nominative by the adverbial phrase, as is permissible in the singular, because the attribute has no pronoun in it. From the fact that "azwaj" is raised as a singular, as Abu Ali said. "Azwaj" means kinds and types of punishment.

Ya'qub said: "al-shakl" with a fatha means "the like," and with a kasra means "al-dall" (coquetry). [It is said: a woman who is "dhat shakl" (with a kasra) means she is coquettish, which is good conversation, good jesting, and bearing.]

His words: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: when the leaders enter the Fire, then the followers enter after them, the guardians say to the leaders: "This is a host," meaning the followers, and "host" is a group. "Rushing in with you" means entering the Fire with you. The leaders said: "No welcome for them!" meaning, may their dwellings in the Fire not be spacious. "Al-rahb" is spaciousness, and from it comes "rahbat al-masjid" (the courtyard of the mosque) and other things. This is in the manner of a supplication, so it is in the accusative. Al-Nabigha said:

*"No welcome for a morning, nor a family in it, though the separation of loved ones is in the morning."*

Abu Ubayda said: the Arabs say: "No welcome for you," meaning, may the earth not be spacious for you and not expanded! ﴿They will burn in the Fire﴾. It was said: this is from the words of the leaders, meaning, they will burn in the Fire as we burned in it. It was also said: this is from the words of the angels, connected to their words: "This is a host rushing in with you." And ﴿They will say: "Rather, you! No welcome for you!"﴾ is from the words of the followers. Al-Naqqash related that the first host were the leaders of the polytheists and those who fed them on the day of Badr, and the second host were their followers at Badr. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is general to every follower and every one followed. ﴿"You brought it upon us, so evil is the abode"﴾, meaning: "You called us to disobedience." ﴿They will say, meaning the followers: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, double his punishment in the Fire"﴾. Al-Farra' said: "whoever made this permissible for us and set it as a custom." Others said: "whoever brought upon us this punishment by calling us to sins." ﴿"Double his punishment in the Fire"﴾: the punishment for his calling us, so that becomes double. Ibn Mas'ud said: the meaning of "double punishment in the Fire" is the serpents and the vipers.

A parallel to this verse is His words: ﴿"Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them double punishment from the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

His son 'Ikrimah has embraced Islam, his daughter Juwayriyah has embraced Islam, his mother has embraced Islam, and his brother has embraced Islam, while he himself has disbelieved.'" He said:

"And a light that illuminated the earth, east and west,
while the place of my foot in it is black and dark."

﴿Did we take them as objects of ridicule?﴾ Mujahid said: "We took them as objects of ridicule in the world, and we were mistaken. ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ so that we do not know where they are." Al-Hasan said: "All of that they did: they took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them in the world, belittling them." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is: "Are they with us in the Fire, so that we do not see them?"

Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿mina al-ashrar ittakhadhnahum﴾ with the alif deleted in connection (wasl). Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾ with the alif of interrogation pronounced (qat'), and the alif of connection dropped, because it has become unnecessary. Whoever reads with the alif deleted does not pause on ﴿al-ashrar﴾, because ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Nahhas and al-Sijistani said: it is a description (na't) of ﴿rijal﴾ (men). Ibn al-Anbari said: this is an error, because a description cannot be in the past or the future tense. Whoever reads ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾ with the alif pronounced stops at ﴿al-ashrar﴾. Al-Farra' said: the interrogation here carries the sense of reproach and wonder. As for ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾: when you read with the interrogative, ﴿am﴾ is for equalization (taswiyah); and when you read without the interrogative, it means "bal" (rather).

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shaybah, al-Mufaddal, Hubayrah, Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿sikhriyyan﴾ with a dammah on the sin. The rest read it with a kasrah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: whoever reads it with a kasrah takes it from mockery (al-huzw), and whoever reads it with a dammah takes it from subjugation (al-taskhir).

It has already been mentioned: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾. ﴿Haqqun﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿takhasum﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a dispute." It may also be a substitute (badal) for ﴿haqqun﴾. It may also be the predicate of a second predicate. It may also be a substitute for ﴿dhalika﴾ according to its position, meaning: indeed the disputing of the people of the Fire in the Fire is true. He means their saying: ﴿"No welcome to you"﴾ and the verse, and similar sayings of the people of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 65–70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "I am only a warner"﴾, meaning a one who frightens [people] with the punishment of Allah those who disobey Him, and this has already been discussed. "And there is no god" meaning no worshipped one "except Allah, the One, the Subduer" who has no partner, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving." It is in the nominative case as an adjective (na't); and if you put the first in the accusative, you put this in the accusative too. It is also permissible to put the first in the nominative and the words after it in the accusative as a term of praise (madh). "Al-'Aziz" means the Invincible, the One having no like. "Al-Ghaffar" means the One who covers the sins of His creatures.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "It is a great news"﴾, meaning: And say to them, O Muhammad, "It is a great news", that is, what I warn you of, the reckoning, the reward and the punishment, is a report of great importance, so it should not be treated lightly. Qatadah said this is its meaning. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it means the Qur'an, which informs you of it, is a glorious report. It was also said: [it is] of great benefit. "You are turning away from it."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing﴾. The Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) are the angels, according to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. They disputed concerning the matter of Adam when he was created, so ﴿they said, "Will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and Iblis said: ﴿"I am better than him"﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. In this is a clarification that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed about the story of Adam and others, and that is not conceivable except through divine support; so the miracle has been established as evidence of his truthfulness. Why then do they turn away from reflecting upon the Qur'an in order to recognize his truthfulness? For this reason He connected His saying with "Say, 'It is a great news, from which you are turning away.'"

A second statement, transmitted by Abu al-Ash'hab from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "My Lord asked me, 'O Muhammad, about what did the Exalted Assembly dispute?' I said, 'About the expiations (kaffarat) and the degrees (darajat).' He said, 'And what are the expiations?' I said, 'Walking on foot to the congregations, perfecting the ablution in severe cold [[al-sabarat is the plural of sabrah, with a sukun on the ba', meaning intense cold]], and waiting for the prayer in the mosques after the prayer.' He said, 'And what are the degrees?' I said, 'Spreading the greeting of peace, feeding food, and praying at night while people are asleep.'" al-Tirmidhi transmitted it in its meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, and said concerning it: "It is a strange hadith." Also from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and he said: "It is a good, sound hadith." We have written it in full in the book al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna, and we have clarified its difficulty, and praise be to Allah. The discussion of walking to the mosques has already passed in [the commentary on] Ya-Sin [[See p. 12 onwards of this part.]], and that steps erase sins and raise degrees.

It was also said: the Exalted Assembly are the angels, and the pronoun in "they dispute" refers to two groups, meaning the statement of those among them who said the angels are the daughters of Allah, and those who said they are gods to be worshipped [[An addition required by the context, mentioned by Abu Hayyan in his tafsir.]]. It was also said: the Exalted Assembly here are Quraysh, meaning their disputing among themselves in secret, and Allah informed His Prophet of that.

﴿"It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner"﴾, meaning: it is only revealed to me to warn. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "illa innama" with a kasrah on the hamzah, because revelation is speech, as if it were said: "It is said to me, 'You are only a clear warner.'" Whoever opened it made it in the position of the nominative, since it is the subject of what has not been named as agent (ism ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Al-Farra' said: It is as if you said: "What is revealed to me is only the warning." Al-Nahhas said: It may also be in the position of the accusative, meaning "illa li-annama." And Allah knows best.

Why then do they turn away from reflecting upon the Qur'an in order to recognize his truthfulness? For this reason He connected His saying with "Say, 'It is a great news, from which you are turning away.'"

A second statement, transmitted by Abu al-Ash'hab from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "My Lord asked me, 'O Muhammad, about what did the Exalted Assembly dispute?' I said, 'About the expiations (kaffarat) and the degrees (darajat).' He said, 'And what are the expiations?' I said, 'Walking on foot to the congregations, perfecting the ablution in severe cold [[al-sabarat is the plural of sabrah, with a sukun on the ba', meaning intense cold]], and waiting for the prayer in the mosques after the prayer.' He said, 'And what are the degrees?' I said, 'Spreading the greeting of peace, feeding food, and praying at night while people are asleep.'" al-Tirmidhi transmitted it in its meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, and said concerning it: "It is a strange hadith." Also from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and he said: "It is a good, sound hadith." We have written it in full in the book al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna, and we have clarified its difficulty, and praise be to Allah. The discussion of walking to the mosques has already passed in [the commentary on] Ya-Sin [[See p. 12 onwards of this part.]], and that steps erase sins and raise degrees.

It was also said: the Exalted Assembly are the angels, and the pronoun in "they dispute" refers to two groups, meaning the statement of those among them who said the angels are the daughters of Allah, and those who said they are gods to be worshipped [[An addition required by the context, mentioned by Abu Hayyan in his tafsir.]]. It was also said: the Exalted Assembly here are Quraysh, meaning their disputing among themselves in secret, and Allah informed His Prophet of that.

﴿"It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner"﴾, meaning: it is only revealed to me to warn. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "illa innama" with a kasrah on the hamzah, because revelation is speech, as if it were said: "It is said to me, 'You are only a clear warner.'" Whoever opened it made it in the position of the nominative, since it is the subject of what has not been named as agent (ism ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Al-Farra' said: It is as if you said: "What is revealed to me is only the warning." Al-Nahhas said: It may also be in the position of the accusative, meaning "illa li-annama." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verses 71–74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾. "Idh" (when) is connected to "yakhtasimun" (dispute), meaning: I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) when they disputed, when "your Lord said to the angels: Indeed I am creating a human from clay." It was also said: "idh qala" is a substitute (badal) for "idh yakhtasimun," and "yakhtasimun" is governed by an omitted element (mahdhuf), because the meaning is: I had no knowledge of the speech of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their disputing.

"Fa-idha sawwaytuhu" (So when I have fashioned him): "idha" (when) turns the past tense toward the future, because it resembles the particles of conditional (huruf al-shart), and its response is like its response, i.e., "I created him."

"And I breathed into him of My spirit" (wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi): that is, of the spirit which I possess and which none other than I possesses. This is the meaning of the idafah (attribution), and this meaning has already been explained thoroughly in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 6, p. 22 onward, first or second edition.]] in His saying concerning Jesus: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [An-Nisa: 171].

"Fa-qa'u lahu sajidin" (Then fall down before him in prostration): accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). This is the prostration of greeting (sujud tahiyyah), not the prostration of worship (sujud 'ibadah), and it has been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 293, second or third edition.]].

"Fa-sajada al-malaikatu kulluhum ajma'un" (So the angels prostrated, all of them together): that is, they carried out the command and prostrated to him, submitting to him and glorifying God by glorifying Him. "Illa Iblis" (except Iblis): he was too proud to prostrate to him, out of ignorance that prostrating to him was obedience to God, and that refusing to obey God out of arrogance is disbelief; for this reason he was among the disbelievers by his arrogance toward the command of God, Exalted is He. The discussion of this has already been completed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 296 onward, second or third edition.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 38, verse 75–83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?"﴾ That is, what diverted and barred you, "from prostrating" — that is, from prostrating — "to what I created with My hands." He attributed His creation to Himself as an honour for it, although He is the Creator of all things. This is like His attributing to Himself the Spirit, the House, the she-camel and the mosques. He addressed the people in terms they understand from their own dealings, for a leader among created beings does not handle anything with his hand except as a sign of magnification and honour, so the mention of the hand here carries this meaning. Mujahid said: "The hand here means emphasis and connection; its metaphorical sense is 'what I Myself created,' like His saying: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], meaning 'your Lord remains.'" It is also said: the comparison of the hand in the creation of God, may He be exalted, is evidence that it does not mean blessing, strength or power, but that they are two attributes of His essence, exalted be He. It is also said: by the hand He meant power, as one says, "I have no hand (yad) in this matter," and "I have no two hands (yadan) for this heavy load." This is supported by the fact that creation occurs only through power, by consensus. The poet said:

"I have taken upon myself from ʿAfra' [in the original texts: Dhalfa', which is a distortion; the verse is by ʿUrwa ibn Hizam] what is not mine to bear — for the towering mountains have no hands (yadan)."

It is also said: "to what I created with My hands" means to what I created without an intermediary. "Have you become arrogant" — that is, from prostrating — "or were you among the exalted?" — that is, among those who are proud over your Lord. Muhammad ibn Salih, from Shibl, from Ibn Kathir and the people of Mecca, read "by My hands, have you become arrogant?" with the alif joined, as a statement; and then "am" is disjunctive, meaning "rather," like His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has forged it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3] and the like. Whoever reads it as a question, then "am" is coordinated with the interrogative hamzah, and it is affirmation and rebuke: "Have you become arrogant within yourself when you refused to prostrate to Adam, or were you among the people who are proud, so that you became proud on this account?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "I am better than him."﴾ Al-Farra' said: Among the Arabs there are those who say "I am better (akhyar) than him and worse (ashurr) than him," and this is the original form, except that it was elided because of frequent use. "You created me from fire and You created him from clay" — he preferred fire over clay, and this was ignorance on his part, for substances are homogeneous, so he analogised and erred in the analogy. Its explanation has already passed in "al-A'raf" [see vol. 7, p. 171, first or second edition]. ﴿He said, "Then get out of it"﴾ — meaning from Paradise — ﴿"for you are accursed"﴾ — that is, stoned with the stars and the meteors. ﴿"And indeed upon you is My curse"﴾ — that is, My expulsion and removal from My mercy — ﴿"until the Day of Recompense."﴾ This is a description of his persistence in disbelief, for the curse then ends; then, by his entering the Fire, the realisation of the curse becomes manifest. ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ The accursed one wanted not to die, so he was not answered in that, but was granted respite until a known time, which is the day on which all creation dies; he was given respite until then, as a sign of contempt for him. ﴿He said, "Then by Your might, I will surely mislead them all"﴾ — when He expelled him because of Adam, he swore by God's might that he would lead the children of Adam astray by adorning desires for them and introducing doubt upon them. So the meaning of "I will surely mislead them" is "I will surely invite them to sins," and he knew that he could reach only to whisper, and would corrupt only those who would not be upright even had he not whispered to them. For this reason He said: ﴿"Except Your sincere servants among them."﴾ That is, those whom You have made sincere for Your worship and whom You have protected from me. Its explanation has already passed in "al-Hijr" [see vol. 10, p. 28, first or second edition].

The Almighty said: ﴿He said, "Then the truth, and the truth I say"﴾. This is the recitation (qira'a) of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), of the people of Basra, and of al-Kisa'i. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, 'Asim, al-A'mash and Hamza recited the first word with a nominative ending (raf'). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive (khafd) for it. There is no disagreement about the second word, that it is in the accusative (nasb) as the object of "aqulu" (I say). The accusative of the first word is by way of incitement (ighra'), meaning: follow the truth and listen to the truth. The second is by way of the saying falling upon it. It is also said that it means: "uhiqqu al-haqq", that is, I will make the truth true, i.e., I will do it. Abu Ali said: The first al-haqq is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning "yuhiqqu Allah al-haqq" (God will establish the truth), or it is in an oath construction, with the preposition of the oath omitted, as you say: "Allahi la-af'alanna" (By God, I will surely do it). Its sense is: "qala fa-bil-haqqi", and al-Haqq is God Almighty, who swore by Himself. "Wa-al-haqqa aqulu" is a clause inserted between the oath and what is sworn to, and it serves to emphasise the account. When al-haqq is made accusative by a hidden verb, "la-amla'anna" stands in the sense of an oath. Al-Farra' and Abu Ubayda also permitted that al-haqq be accusative in the sense of "haqqan" (truly): "la-amla'anna jahannam". According to a group of grammarians, this is an error, since it is not permissible to say "Zaydan la-adribanna", because what follows the lam is cut off from what precedes it and so cannot be governed by it. On their view the construction is: "la-amla'anna jahannama haqqan" (I will surely fill Hell, truly). Whoever reads "fa-al-haqqu" with the nominative makes it the subject of a nominal sentence, meaning: "fa-ana al-haqqu" (so I am the truth) or "al-haqqu minni" (the truth is from me). Both are narrated from Mujahid. It is also permissible that the sense is: "hadha al-haqq" (this is the truth). A third view, according to the school of Sibawayh and al-Farra', is that the meaning of "fa-al-haqqu la-amla'anna jahannama" is "fa-al-haqqu an amla'a jahannama" (so the truth is that I will fill Hell). As for the genitive, there are two views, and it is the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqa and Talha ibn Musarrif. One is that it is by omission of the particle of oath; this is the view of al-Farra', who said: as one says, "Allahi 'azza wa-jalla la-af'alanna" (By God, Mighty and Majestic, I will surely do it). Sibawayh permitted such a construction, but Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) considered it an error and did not permit the genitive, because particles of the genitive are not elided. The other view is that the fa' is a substitute for the waw of oath, as they cited in verse: [Imru' al-Qays, from his Mu'allaqa, whose complete line is: "fa-alhaytuha 'an dhi tama'imin muhawwali" (so I distracted her from the one with amulets, the nursling). The rest is missing.]:

"fa-mithlika hublan qad taraqtu wa-murdi'in" (By the likes of you, I have visited the pregnant and the nursing woman).

"La-amla'anna jahannama minka", that is, from you yourself and your offspring, "wa-mimman tabi'aka" (and from those who follow you) "min Bani Adam" (of the children of Adam) "ajma'in" (all of them).

The Almighty said: ﴿Say, "I do not ask of you any wage for it"﴾, that is, any reward for conveying the revelation. He referred to it by pronoun without mentioning what it refers to. It is also said that it refers back to His saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8]. "Wa-ma ana mina al-mutakallifin" (And I am not of those who pretend), that is, I do not impose upon myself, nor do I speculate about what I have not been commanded. Masruq narrated from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: Whoever is asked about what he does not know, let him say, "I do not know," and not pretend, for saying "I do not know" is knowledge. God Almighty said to His Prophet (ﷺ): "Say, I do not ask of you any wage for it, and I am not of those who pretend." It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The one who pretends has three signs: he disputes with one above him, he reaches for what he cannot attain, and he says what he does not know." Al-Daraqutni narrated, from the hadith of Nafi' from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out on one of his journeys, and he travelled by night. They passed by a man sitting beside his cistern (maqrah) [al-maqrah: the basin in which water gathers. Al-Nihaya of Ibn al-Athir]. "Wa-ma ana mina al-mutakallifin" (And I am not of those who pretend), that is, I do not impose upon myself, nor do I speculate about what I have not been commanded. Masruq narrated from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: Whoever is asked about what he does not know, let him say, "I do not know," and not pretend, for saying "I do not know" is knowledge. God Almighty said to His Prophet (ﷺ): "Say, I do not ask of you any wage for it, and I am not of those who pretend." It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The one who pretends has three signs: he disputes with one above him, he reaches for what he cannot attain, and he says what he does not know." Al-Daraqutni narrated, from the hadith of Nafi' from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out on one of his journeys, and he travelled by night. They passed by a man sitting beside his cistern (maqrah) [al-maqrah: the basin in which water gathers. Al-Nihaya of Ibn al-Athir]. Umar said to him: "O owner of the cistern, have beasts of prey drunk from your cistern tonight?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O owner of the cistern, do not inform him of this, for he is pretending. What they carried in their bellies is theirs, and what remains is drink and purification for us." In the Muwatta' [of Malik], from Yahya ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Hatib: Umar ibn al-Khattab set out in a company among whom was Amr ibn al-As, until they came to a pool. Amr ibn al-As said: "O owner of the pool, do beasts of prey come to your pool?" Umar said: "O owner of the pool, do not inform us, for we come to beasts of prey and they come to us." The discussion of waters has already passed in Surat al-Furqan [see vol. 13, p. 45, first or second edition]. ﴿It is but a Reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿to the worlds﴾, of jinn and humankind. ﴿And you will surely know its news after a time﴾, that is, the news of the Reminder, which is the Qur'an, that it is true, ﴿after a time﴾. Qatada said: after death. Al-Zajjaj said, and Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Ibn Zayd said: meaning the Day of Resurrection. Al-Farra' said: after death and before it, that is, the reality of what I say will become manifest to you. "After a time", that is, in the future, when the swords of the Muslims seize you. Al-Suddi said: that is the Day of Badr. Al-Hasan used to say: O son of Adam, at death the certain news will come to you. Ikrima was asked about one who swore that he would do such-and-such "ila hin" (until a time). He said: Among "hin" is that which cannot be grasped, as in His saying: "And you will surely know its news after a time," and among it is that which can be grasped, as in His saying: ﴿It yields its produce every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25], from the cutting of the palm's dates until its ripening, six months. The discussion of this has already passed in al-Baqara [see vol. 1, p. 321 onwards, second or third edition] and Ibrahim [see vol. 9, p. 360 onwards, first or second edition], and praise be to God.
